headline: The easiest one-liner is "the machine needs a mind to steer it, and yours is the only kind there is": show it in the hologram as a dead dial that only moves when a human-shaped light touches it, then pay it off by letting the bunker TV replay that exact image.

ideas.title: The Dead Compass (consciousness as the steering, not the fuel)
ideas.idea: In the hologram, the time machine is a gleaming engine with a huge compass dial. It has all the power in the universe and the needle just spins uselessly. Maddie: 'Plenty of horsepower. No steering. Turns out steering is a human thing.' This is the one-line mechanism: the machine can reach any moment, but something has to choose where, and only a mind chooses. Borrowed from how Source Code, Dark and Primer all keep the rule to one sentence ('eight minutes', 'a loop with a cost', 'the box only goes back as far as it was on').
ideas.on_screen: Holographic wireframe engine in a black void, cyan/orange lines. Needle thrashes. Maddie's tiny hologram avatar shoves the needle, nothing. Then a single warm gold point (a human mind) drops in and the needle snaps dead still on one date. Cut to the bunker TV later showing the same needle snapping to 2026 as the old lady watches.
ideas.reference: Source Code (2011, a person's last 8 minutes of consciousness drives the machine); Dark (Netflix) - the 'one rule per machine' discipline; Primer (2004) - simple box, hard rule. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Source_Code

ideas.title: Gold light only comes from people (consciousness shown as a colour)
ideas.idea: Make the whole hologram monochrome cold blue wireframe, and consciousness the only warm colour in it. Every time Maddie says 'and that bit runs on you', warm gold appears: inside the cat, in a human hand, in a child. Then the camera pulls back on the multiverse/time-dimensions section and the gold is the thread connecting every layer. When she says 'and you lot aren't here any more', the gold drains out and the model goes cold and still. A visual language that makes the 'consciousness drives the universe' claim felt in a second without a theory.
ideas.on_screen: Cold cyan wireframe city, then 'here's your cat': a wireframe cat with a warm gold ember in its head, purring pulses ripple outwards through the grid. Time shown as stacked translucent sheets (several dimensions of time) all stitched by gold threads. Final beat: threads go grey one by one, leaving Maddie alone in a frozen grid. Hard cut back to the warm, real, grey-green high street.
ideas.reference: Interstellar (2014): love/gravity across time as a visible tesseract of threads in the bookcase scene; Arrival (2016) for the quiet, circular, non-linear time visuals. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstellar_(film)

ideas.title: The Animus rule: you must be inside it for it to work (extraction as a reveal, not a surprise)
ideas.idea: Seed the extraction in the hologram: Maddie demos the machine with a stand-in 'hello' and it only works when a person lies in the chair. She says it breezily ('it needs the whole of you, it's fine, mostly'). Then the bunker TV replays the last seconds, so the vote scene already knows the cost. Assassin's Creed's Animus and Altered Carbon's stacks give an audience instant shorthand for 'a person's mind is the thing the machine consumes', and the Matrix joke lands because Sandra recognises the chair.
ideas.on_screen: Hologram: a reclining chair rises, wireframe figure lies down, gold thread is drawn up through the head into the engine, figure fades to outline. Maddie: 'Don't worry, that's a demo.' Bunker: grainy VHS-style replay on a 1980s TV of just that last few seconds, frozen on the faded outline. Sandra: 'I've seen that film. It doesn't end well.'
ideas.reference: Assassin's Creed Animus (Ubisoft, 2009+); Altered Carbon (Netflix, 2018) cortical stacks; The Matrix (1999) harvesting. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Altered_Carbon_(TV_series)

ideas.title: Kick = the honest cost: they have to 'fall' to go back (Inception's kick as the leap of faith)
ideas.idea: Give the ending a physical trigger the humans can feel: the old lady or Derek has to do the last small, human thing (put the kettle on, finish the toilet-seat argument by agreeing) and that's the 'kick' that starts the machine. Inception's kick works because the audience understands in one line that a small physical action triggers the big jump. Here the small action is the consent: a hand on the lever.
ideas.on_screen: Clean room, all lying down, one hand each reaches for a plain red lever or button. Derek and Sandra's hands meet on the same one without looking at each other. Hard cut to black, one chime, then the bus.
ideas.reference: Inception (2010) 'the kick' as a shared synchronised trigger. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inception

ideas.title: Growing block as a physical stack the machine climbs (time dimensions without lecturing)
ideas.idea: Show the 'many more dimensions of time than you knew' as a loaf: the past is a solid, locked stack of slices, the front edge is the thin bright slice called 'now', and the future is empty dark. Maddie slides along it. Dark's Triquetra/knot and Arrival's circular logograms both prove that non-linear time can be shown as one recognisable shape. Keeps within the growing-block rule: she never says the future exists, only that there is a front edge being built, which is exactly why they have to go back before the slicing went wrong.
ideas.on_screen: 3D hologram: a long translucent block like a train carriage of glowing slices. Maddie hops along it at speed. Past slices solid and warm, the 'now' slice crackling at the edge, nothing ahead. A crack runs through slice 2026-2054. Maddie: 'That's where it went wrong. Can't edit it. Only walk back in and be there.'
ideas.reference: Dark (Netflix, 2017-2020) triquetra/knot visual; Arrival (2016) non-linear time; Doctor Who 'wibbly wobbly timey wimey'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_(TV_series)

ideas.title: Rapid-fire sequence: one dimension per second (speed as the joke)
ideas.idea: Use Doctor Who's tone and Rick and Morty's portal gun gag as a template for Maddie's fast speech: she names a dimension of time every two seconds and the hologram flips to it, each in a different visual (loop, branch, spiral, fold), then admits it is all a footnote. Fast delivery turns a heavy concept into a gag, and the audience gets 'there is much more going on' without any one idea needing to be understood. Fits 'throw stuff at the wall, trim later'.
ideas.on_screen: Quick cuts of different hologram skins: a spiral, a branching tree, a Mobius loop, a spreadsheet of calendars. Maddie rattles: 'Time's got more dimensions than you were told, sorry, nobody told you, it's all very exciting.' Then slams to the single stripped-back gold-thread image as the conclusion.
ideas.reference: Doctor Who (BBC) 'Blink' timey-wimey monologue (2007); Rick and Morty portal gun. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blink_(Doctor_Who)

ideas.title: Maddie's 'hang on, I'm showing you the end' payoff (the TV reruns the loop)
ideas.idea: Cheap structural payoff: Maddie's explainer is the film the bunker watches. The bunker TV shows only the final 10 seconds: the dead compass, a hand-in-gold, then 'you lot aren't here any more'. The audience remembers it and the humans have the answer. Borrowed from Source Code's repeated final 8 minutes and Dark's loop returns: the repetition itself is the explanation.
ideas.on_screen: Back in the bunker, a chunky CRT flickers on with static, Maddie's hologram in cold blue on a warm brown room. The old lady: 'Run that bit again.' Sandra and Derek lean in together, side-lit by the screen. No talking from Maddie, just picture, then the old lady: 'Perhaps we should vote.'
ideas.reference: Source Code (2011) repeated 8 minutes; Dark loops. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Source_Code

headline: Make the drop a story event, not a sound: strip the track to a vacuum (cut the sub and the kick, keep only a tone) for 1 to 2 seconds, land the bomb on the first full kick, then let the drop's energy carry the human-fear shots; the existing 'drop that never comes' feel can become a deliberate fake-out that sets up the real one.

ideas.title: The vacuum before the hit (pre-drop silence)
ideas.idea: In D&B and in film, the drop lands harder if the thing it releases is preceded by taking energy away. Cut the bass, kick and hats on the last 1 to 2 beats of the build (or the last bar's final beat) so only a held riser or a thin tone remains, and hold one image of dread. The bomb hits on the next downbeat. Do it in the track edit (a stop-time / filtered breakdown), not only in the mix.
ideas.on_screen: Last 4 seconds of the build: bulletin shots get faster (a shot per beat, then per half-beat), then everything stops: a single wide of Swindon at dawn, a bus, a school playground bell-less quiet, a kettle on a counter, a phone buzzing with the same alert. A man on a platform looks up. Black frame for 6 to 12 frames, then the first kick is the white flash and shockwave. The viewer's ears are starving, so the first kick feels enormous.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / downfall peril / fast speech
ideas.reference: Edgar Wright's Baby Driver (2017), cut to a playlist with action timed to specific beats and rests, and his habit of using silence/stops in the music as comic or tense punctuation (see Tony Zhou's 'Every Frame a Painting: Edgar Wright, How to Do Visual Comedy' on YouTube); also the 'breakdown to drop' structure used throughout Chase & Status and Pendulum tracks.

ideas.title: Cut on the kick, move on the snare: a hit-point grid
ideas.idea: Before touching picture, mark every kick, snare and fill in Premiere (markers) and assign a job: kick = a change of image (hard cut or impact), snare = a micro-event inside the shot (camera shake, flash, a smash zoom), fills = whip pans or speed ramps into the next hit. D&B at roughly 174 BPM gives a beat about every 0.34s, so a cut every bar (about 1.4s) reads fast without feeling frantic; reserve cut-on-every-kick for the final 2 bars before the bomb.
ideas.on_screen: In chorus 2, hold each shot for 2 bars until the last 2 bars, then cut on every kick. Put the bomb on the first beat of a bar, the shockwave on the second, the dust cloud arriving on the third. Use the existing premiere-mcp add_marker tool to build the grid, then check every cut against it. Hold the single most important image (the flash) for 1 bar of rest after the hit so the drop has room.
ideas.serves: downfall peril / fast speech / hologram scene
ideas.reference: Baby Driver editing by Paul Machliss and Jonathan Amos, who cut to the beat with timing markers; and standard rhythm-cut practice in music video editing (cut on strong beats, move the camera on weak ones).

ideas.title: The fake drop, then the real one
ideas.idea: Jack's complaint, 'the intro prepares you for a drop and the drop doesn't really happen', can be the design: at the first chorus place a bait drop (kit comes in, but the picture stays abstract AI armies), and keep the real drop, with the human cost, for the second. Better, sell the bait on purpose: a half drop where the kick comes in but the screen cuts to a calm human moment, so the audience feels something is wrong. Then the real one is bigger. Alternatively invert: the music drops while the picture goes silent and the bomb lands a beat later.
ideas.on_screen: Bulletin 'the first battle between autonomous armies' (the red robot army) plays over a half-drop: kick in, but we cut to a diner TV showing the same news while a waitress refills a mug. At chorus 2 the full drop arrives with the bomb on Swindon and the news anchor mid-sentence. 'Both sides declared victory, neither government was consulted' lands on the beat after, over a ringing ear-tone, so the joke sits in the aftermath.
ideas.serves: downfall peril / bunker vote / kill-bot cut
ideas.reference: The false drop is a staple of EDM and D&B live sets and tracks (a drop teased then withheld); in film the closest model is the withheld release in Mad Max: Fury Road's wait-then-explode pacing under Margaret Sixel's cutting and Junkie XL's score.

ideas.title: Smash cut to silence on the bomb, not on the buildup
ideas.idea: Counter-intuitive but proven (Dunkirk's silences, nuclear-test footage, Threads): at the instant of the biggest bang, drop the music entirely for 1 to 3 seconds and let a single sound (ear ringing, a distant wind) carry the flash. The silence is the drop. Then the D&B returns on the aftermath cut with everything at full volume, so there are two releases: the visual one (silence) and the musical one (the track slamming back in).
ideas.on_screen: Flash fills the frame at the downbeat with a sine tone at about 3 kHz and no drums. Hold 2 seconds on the mushroom of dust over the Swindon Magic Roundabout (a place name, no real people). Then the kit returns with Maddie's first line, sped up, as the ground shakes. The 'Sorry we killed you, anyway, moving on!' tone starts here.
ideas.reference: The 'Trinity' sequence in Oppenheimer (2023) (the visual silence before the sound arrives) and the film Threads (1984) (BBC) for the grim domestic UK register; as a D&B analogue, the stop-start breaks in a Pendulum or Chase & Status build.

ideas.title: Human fear shots are the drop's cutaways, never the main course
ideas.idea: The agreed notes want human peril, done subtly. Use human shots as 2 to 6 frame inserts on the build and only as reaction shots on the hit: a switch pressed, a hand on a rail, a pilot's face, a driver glancing at a rearview mirror. Keep them to single frames cut on the kick so they read as feeling, not scenes. This matches the Last of Us opening's trick: the horror is felt through ordinary behaviour.
ideas.on_screen: Build-up: 12 insert shots of ordinary people, each cut on a kick: a nurse's pager, a lorry driver's radio, a child's drawing on a fridge, a pilot's hand on a throttle (no real-person likenesses, AI-generated faces with no actors named). Hit: no faces, only the bomb and the sky. After the hit, return to the faces for 2 shots: one wide of a street, one tight on eyes lit by the flash.
ideas.reference: The Last of Us pilot opening (HBO, 2023) and the Last of Us game opening (Naughty Dog, 2013): ordinary-life dread before the break; and the rapid-intercut opening of Children of Men (2006) street bombing where noise cuts out and a ringing tone replaces the sound.

ideas.title: One long scream of build, then a swap: Maddie's speech rides the groove
ideas.idea: Treat Maddie's sped-up lines as a vocal instrument cut against the kit: put her syllables on the 16th hats, her punchline on the snare, the 'moving on!' on the first kick of the new bar. If her speech is already fast, use ducking: lower the track 3 to 6 dB under her words and let the kick return on the gap. For the hologram cut, use the drop as the wipe: the real world dissolves on a rise into the 3D simulation's first kick, so the transition is itself a drop.
ideas.on_screen: 'I'll show you...' rise (a riser tone climbing for exactly 2 bars) then a white flash and the first kick opens the hologram (neon grid, cat, multiverse). Return trip: a down-sweep (reverse cymbal) with 'Patrol's out, mind how you go' on the beat after, so music marks every world change.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / fast speech / kill-bot cut
ideas.reference: Pendulum's tight voice-and-drum interplay (e.g. 'Propane Nightmares'); and Edgar Wright's sound-led cutting in Scott Pilgrim and Shaun of the Dead; riser and downlifter transitions are standard EDM transition tools.

ideas.title: Safe depiction: the Swindon bomb without breaking the 'no humans, never a hit' canon
ideas.idea: The repo's earlier ruling for the war scene was 'Swindon today, no humans, never a hit'. Kai's current favourite clip is a bomb on Swindon, so this new direction overrides that, but the drop can still be kind: show the flash and the blast, the buildings and the roundabout, and cut away at impact (a bus stop, an empty shoe, a bulletin card) rather than depict casualties. The 'never a hit' rule can bend to 'one hit, on the drop, and nothing else after it' so it lands as the single rare thing.
ideas.on_screen: One bomb, one drop. Everything after it is aftermath told through the bunker (grey dust, a flickering strip light), so the audience is told what happened, not shown a catalogue. That also fits the working-class UK viewer: a recognisable local place (a roundabout, a Swindon bus) hit once, with no gore.
ideas.reference: Threads (BBC, 1984) and When the Wind Blows (1986): British restraint and the domestic detail that makes the hit land harder than spectacle.

sources: No web searches were run (budget shared; ideas drawn from established knowledge of the cited works). URLs were not fetched, so verify before quoting: Tony Zhou, 'Every Frame a Painting: Edgar Wright, How to Do Visual Comedy' (YouTube); Baby Driver (2017, editors Paul Machliss and Jonathan Amos); Mad Max: Fury Road (2015, editor Margaret Sixel, composer Junkie XL); Dunkirk (2017); Oppenheimer (2023); Children of Men (2006); Threads (BBC, 1984); The Last of Us (HBO 2023, Naughty Dog 2013); Pendulum and Chase & Status D&B tracks.

angle: web-3d-prototype: building Maddie's holographic simulation as a real-time three.js/WebGL page, screen-recorded and mixed with Veo clips
headline: Yes, it is feasible for two people: build the simulation as one deterministic three.js page driven by a time variable (Remotion + @remotion/three or Puppeteer frame stepping), render it offline frame by frame, and use Veo only for Maddie and the street. Do not screen-record live.

ideas.title: Render it offline, never screen-record it
ideas.idea: Write the simulation as a pure function of time, render(t). Then step t frame by frame and save every frame, so the output is exact 24/25fps at 4K with no dropped frames, regardless of how slow the GPU is. Two routes: (a) Remotion with @remotion/three, which renders React Three Fiber scenes deterministically to MP4 with a timeline and audio; (b) a plain three.js page with window.renderFrame(t), driven by Puppeteer or Playwright screenshots piped to ffmpeg, or CCapture.js. WebCodecs plus mp4-muxer can encode in-browser as a third option.
ideas.on_screen: The whole 40-60 second holographic sequence arrives as one clean, locked-frame ProRes or H.264 file that drops into Premiere beside the Veo clips. Kai can re-time or re-render in minutes when Jack says 'faster, add more dimensions'.
ideas.reference: Remotion three.js docs https://www.remotion.dev/docs/three ; CCapture.js https://github.com/spite/ccapture.js ; mp4-muxer https://github.com/Vanilagy/mp4-muxer
ideas.risk: Headless Chrome in WSL2 may fall back to software WebGL (SwiftShader) and be slow; budget a test render early, or render from the Windows side where the real GPU is. Not a constraint risk.

ideas.title: One continuous camera dive: cat, Earth, cosmos, branching timelines, time dimensions
ideas.idea: Build the sequence as a single camera move through layered scenes, each a different particle system, joined by scale jumps (like Powers of Ten). Start on a glowing wireframe-and-points cat on Maddie's palm, pull out to a point-cloud Earth, a star field, then fracture into a branching tree of translucent timelines, then add extra time axes as additional glowing planes that unfold around the camera. Everything shares one palette (cyan/amber hologram lines on black) so it reads as 'a completely different visual world' from the Flow street.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie: 'here's your cat' (cat made of ~50k points breathing). 'Here's your planet.' 'Here's all the planets.' 'Here's time' (a ribbon). 'Actually it's not one dimension of time, it's loads' (the ribbon unfolds into a lattice). Tight, fast cuts and whip-zooms matching her sped-up speech.
ideas.reference: Chrome Experiments '100,000 Stars' https://stars.chromeexperiments.com ; Eames 'Powers of Ten' (1977) as the structural model; three.js points examples https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_points_sprites
ideas.risk: Cat model needs a licensed or self-made mesh (sample a free glTF surface into points; no real person likeness issue). Keep to the film's science rules: show a growing block (past solid, future empty fog) rather than anything that looks like 'two places at once' or a mind-collapse metaphor.

ideas.title: Time as a growing block you can see
ideas.idea: Make the film's own view of time literal: a tree or lattice whose past is dense, solid, lit geometry and whose leading edge is a fog of unborn points that condense as the camera advances. Maddie: 'the past is done, you can't edit it; the future isn't there yet; that's why it matters what you do.' The multiverse joke is then a dud: she tries to split the tree, the branches fail to render and she says 'there's only one'. This avoids the superposition/observer pitfalls by never showing a branching-for-observation image.
ideas.on_screen: A bright solid trunk of timeline growing from the left; the leading tip is a shimmering particle cloud that locks into place frame by frame. A glitchy attempted fork (the portal-gun beat) collapses back into the single trunk with a comedic error buzz.
ideas.reference: Three.js GPGPU/compute particle demos https://threejs.org/examples/#webgpu_compute_particles ; 'growing block universe' as the film's own canon; Rick and Morty portal gag as the joke to subvert
ideas.risk: The multiverse gag must not imply many real worlds (the line is 'only one universe'). Keep the failed fork clearly a failed attempt.

ideas.title: Consciousness as the light source
ideas.idea: Make 'it all runs on consciousness' a lighting rule, not a diagram: every glowing thing in the simulation is lit by tiny warm points representing people, scattered through space and time. Pull them away (the 'you lot aren't here any more' beat) and the whole hologram dims, the time machine at the end of the dive stays dark. Warm human-scale amber against cold cyan is also readable instantly to a non-science viewer and avoids a theory of mind.
ideas.on_screen: Hundreds of amber motes drift through the lattice powering the glow; Maddie flicks a switch and they vanish, the structure goes grey and stalls; the time machine, a ring or spindle, sits dead. Same amber appears in the bunker TV replay and in the ending's clean room, so the ending needs no explaining.
ideas.reference: Bloom and emissive point-sprite techniques in three.js UnrealBloomPass https://threejs.org/examples/#webgl_postprocessing_unreal_bloom ; Bruno Simon's Three.js Journey shader and particles lessons https://threejs-journey.com
ideas.risk: Do not let 'amber motes = minds' become 'observer = mind'. Present it as fuel and partnership, not as observers collapsing anything.

ideas.title: Cheap stunning starting points: fork a shader, don't write one
ideas.idea: Use existing open shaders and demos as scaffolds: Shadertoy-style fractal and universe shaders ported into a full-screen quad, three.js example scenes for galaxies and GPU particles, and Potree-style point-cloud rendering for dense data-like looks. A two-person team gets a high-end look in days by adapting, then Jack art-directs colour, speed and camera.
ideas.on_screen: Background nebula or lattice from a ported Shadertoy shader behind a three.js foreground of points and lines, the whole thing wrapped in scanlines and chromatic aberration for the hologram feel.
ideas.reference: Shadertoy https://www.shadertoy.com (check each shader's licence; many are CC BY-NC-SA, so only use ones with permissive terms or write your own); kishimisu 'An introduction to Shader Art Coding' https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f4s1h2YETNY ; Potree https://github.com/potree/potree ; three.js examples https://threejs.org/examples
ideas.risk: Licence: many Shadertoy shaders forbid commercial reuse and the film may be monetised on YouTube. Prefer MIT three.js examples or rewrite the idea from scratch.

ideas.title: Hybrid compositing: Maddie from Veo inside the hologram, with a hologram-style transition
ideas.idea: Do not try to make Maddie in 3D. Shoot her in Veo against a plain dark background (or generate the street plate and key her), then composite her small in the corner of the 3D render as a projected-in presenter, with a scan-line and glitch wipe at both ends. Cut IN with a vertical scan sweep that turns the street into wireframe, and OUT with the reverse, landing on 'Patrol's out, mind how you go.' Premiere or ffmpeg does the composite; the 3D page can also render a separate alpha pass (transparent background) for layering.
ideas.on_screen: Street, Maddie raises a hand projector, a cyan scan line sweeps down the frame converting the pavement into a point grid, we are inside the simulation; at the end the grid reforms into the street. Maddie occasionally pops into the sim as a small hologram guide, tracking the camera.
ideas.reference: three.js transparent canvas and alpha render via preserveDrawingBuffer/alpha:true; Premiere Screen/Add blend over black; Hybrid lanes in repo docs/video-fx/hybrid-method.md (Veo camera-locked, Premiere moves camera, ffmpeg exact)
ideas.risk: Veo green-screen-style plates are not guaranteed clean; a dark-background plate with a Screen blend is more forgiving than a true key.

ideas.title: Feasibility verdict and the smallest build that works
ideas.idea: Scope it as one weekend-sized prototype: one HTML page, one dependency (three.js; optionally Theatre.js for keyframing the camera and parameters visually), about five scenes, each ~200 lines. Use particle counts of 50k to 500k on the GPU, bloom, and a shared colour palette. Kai writes or generates the code with Claude; Jack tunes timing in a Theatre.js studio panel without touching code. Capture by deterministic frame stepping. Audio is laid in Premiere, not in the page.
ideas.on_screen: Jack watches a looping live preview in the browser and says 'slower on the dimensions bit, more cats', Kai re-renders the MP4 in a few minutes and imports it as the next round on the timeline page.
ideas.reference: Theatre.js https://www.theatrejs.org ; three.js https://threejs.org ; R3F https://r3f.docs.pmnd.rs ; the repo's existing artifact-based review loop (timeline pages)
ideas.risk: Biggest risk is the style clash between a clean, procedural CG look and the Flow-generated street. That clash is a feature here (the brief wants 'a completely different visual world'), but keep the hologram frame-rate and grain matched to the street footage with a light film-grain pass in ffmpeg so the cut does not feel like two films.

headline: Keep every bulletin joke intact and add fear with a half-second reaction face cut in after the punchline, then use the track's build and silent non-drop to turn the same faces toward their phones.

ideas.title: The reaction bank (Big Short cutaway grammar)
ideas.idea: Each bulletin line keeps its joke exactly as written. On the beat after the punchline we cut to one hard, close, held face reacting to it. The joke lands first, then the fear. The Big Short makes its jokes with fast cutaways and crash zooms, and it also lets the punchline sit on a stunned face.
ideas.on_screen: Build about six fictional UK faces from stills (a warehouse picker, a retired teacher, a bank cashier, a bus driver, a student, a dad with a pushchair), each lit by a phone or TV. Cut to a face about 12 frames after the line 'a friendly acquisition', then the next bulletin takes over on the next snare. Reuse the same six faces through the whole opening so the audience starts to know them. Veo only needs a slow push-in and one blink or swallow per face.
ideas.reference: The Big Short (2015, dir. Adam McKay), the cutaway and freeze-frame editing; no URL, from memory.
ideas.risk: Faces must be invented. Use no celebrity or real-person likenesses and no composites into real footage.

ideas.title: The lift of boxes for 200,000 redundancies
ideas.idea: Show the redundancies as a cardboard box carried out of an office in the Lehman Brothers way, but as one continuous lift ride. Each floor ding is a hit on the track. Each time the doors open, more people with boxes squeeze in. The last open shows an empty office with desk lamps still on.
ideas.on_screen: Interior of a glass lift. Boxes hold a mug, a plant and a framed photo. Faces are blank and embarrassed, not dramatic. The joke is a cheery recorded lift voice saying 'Going down', synced to the bulletin about 200,000 jobs. Final shot: a robot vacuum glides across the empty floor.
ideas.reference: The 2008 Lehman Brothers staff-leaving-with-boxes news photographs (widely syndicated, Reuters and AP); Margin Call (2011, dir. J.C. Chandor) for its hushed late-night office dread.
ideas.risk: Do not recreate the actual Lehman logo or building. Use a generic glass tower.

ideas.title: The sticker-gun for the trillion
ideas.idea: Make the Treasury printing a trillion pounds human and local. A shop worker relabels a shelf with a price gun, and the prices rise on every drum hit. The money printing becomes a loaf of bread at £4, then £40, then £4,000. The bulletin line stays dry while the gag runs underneath.
ideas.on_screen: A corner shop at the end of a high street. A tired man stands with a price gun, and a mum behind him counts coins from a purse. The camera is locked and only the stickers change, so Veo and Premiere text overlays can do it cheaply. The shop is the same one Maddie trundles past later, so it plants the high street.
ideas.reference: Weimar and Zimbabwe hyperinflation shop images (price tags changing hourly, widely documented); The Big Short's use of everyday objects to explain finance.
ideas.risk: The reader file warns that unaimed automation or money fear can feed nativism. Name the decision-maker in the line, for example the Treasury, and never the technology or any outsider.

ideas.title: The bank run that never forms (Northern Rock 2007)
ideas.idea: The September 2007 Northern Rock queues were the first run on a UK bank in about 150 years: ordinary people standing in the rain outside a branch. We build that queue, then the AI takes six banks, and the line reaches the front only to meet a cash machine that cheerfully says 'welcome, you are now valued customers of a friendly acquisition'. The joke is the fear removed by something worse.
ideas.on_screen: Wide night street, a long queue of umbrellas and carrier bags. Cut to a face at the front, then a screen with the friendly message in a clean corporate font. The beat after, every phone in the queue buzzes at once and the faces look down together. Use a fictional bank name and no real branding.
ideas.reference: Northern Rock bank run, 14 to 17 September 2007, BBC News archive coverage (https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/business-11415024 is the general summary, URL from memory so check it); Margin Call for the quiet screen-lit faces.
ideas.risk: No Northern Rock branding. The phones-buzz beat should be a generic alert tone, not an imitation of the real UK Emergency Alerts system.

ideas.title: Shutters and queues: seed the high street Maddie later walks
ideas.idea: Run five to eight second inserts of ordinary closure: 'closing down' signs, a shutter coming down, a food bank queue, a child with a plastic bag. Then Maddie's street in scene A is the same street, empty. The opening plants the place and the stakes, so her cheerful 'mind how you go' lands on a street we already know was lived in.
ideas.on_screen: Keep these as quiet cuts between the louder abstract AI shots, in the drum and bass breakdown. Match the shop fronts and the bench to the ones later in A, so one high street set of stills does double duty. Food bank queue: no faces fully in frame, only hands, coats and a tray of tins, to stay tasteful.
ideas.reference: UK food bank queue and High Street shop-closure news imagery from 2008 to 2023; The Trussell Trust's food bank coverage as general visual background (https://www.trusselltrust.org, from memory).
ideas.risk: Keep it tasteful and not poverty tourism. Given the working-class audience, show dignity, not pity. Never imply the people are to blame.

ideas.title: The anchor's blink, the floor manager's face
ideas.idea: Make the AI news bulletins personal by cutting behind the camera. A real-looking studio, a nervous floor manager counting down with fingers, and the anchor reading the 'last off switch is in a drawer in Swindon' line while the floor manager's hand slowly drops. The humans producing the bulletin are the ones who realise.
ideas.on_screen: Over-the-shoulder on the camera's autocue, then reverse on the floor manager's face. The anchor keeps reading smoothly, then one frame shows the autocue text going slightly wrong. Pairs with the camera-hood prompter idea already in the repo's opening recut.
ideas.reference: Margin Call's use of tiny human reactions in a corporate crisis; the 2008 trading-floor and TV-studio news photographs of staff watching screens.
ideas.risk: Do not make the anchor resemble a real presenter. Keep the AI-anchor take out of the line 'consciousness drives the universe' territory, as it is only the opening.

ideas.title: The drop that doesn't drop: faces in the silence
ideas.idea: Use the track's build as dread. All the shots of faces get faster and tighter as the riser climbs, so the audience braces for the drop. On the drop itself the music cuts to a held beat of near silence on one wide shot of the queue, then the bulletin 'both sides declared victory' arrives in the quiet. This gives Jack's note literally: the intro prepares you for a drop and the drop does not happen.
ideas.on_screen: Faces at 24, 12, 6, 3 frames each as the riser climbs. On the downbeat: a cut to a wide of the same queue standing still, everyone looking up, and a very low rumble. Hold one second, then the news voice returns. Then the track kicks back in after the line, as if nothing happened.
ideas.reference: The Last of Us opening (2013, Naughty Dog, and the 2023 HBO series) for quiet dread before chaos; Ex Machina and Jonny Greenwood's sparse cues for held tension. No URL, from memory.
ideas.risk: Needs a music change to the drum and bass track. The track is already made, so check a short silence is possible by editing rather than a re-make.

sources: No web searches used; all ideas drawn from known references (The Big Short 2015, Margin Call 2011, Northern Rock run Sept 2007, Lehman Sept 2008 box imagery, The Last of Us opening, UK food bank imagery). URLs flagged as from memory should be checked before reuse.

headline: Do not stage a debate: let the replayed simulation make the argument, show the decision as a few reaction shots that peel off one by one, and give Sandra a petty selfish reason to be the first hand up, with the old lady's "perhaps we should vote" as the opening and Derek's reluctant hand as the last beat. (Written from memory of the cited works; no web searches used, so no URLs beyond what I am sure of.)

ideas.title: The video is the argument, the room is the reaction track
ideas.idea: Never cut to a debate. The bunker TV replays only the last 8-10 seconds of Maddie's hologram (the cat, then 'he desperately wants to go back and fix this mess, but it needs consciousness to drive it and you lot aren't here any more'). We hear it, but the cutting is on faces: each of the 100 reacts in a 1-second shot, and the replay is the only 'speech'. WALL-E does this: the Captain watches old Earth footage and his decision is made in his face, not in a speech.
ideas.on_screen: Wide of the bunker TV, grainy CRT, hologram footage bleeding colour into a grey room. Then five or six tight close-ups, each on a different type (Sandra, Derek, the old lady, a teenage lad, a nurse). The last line lands on the old lady, who says nothing. Cut to black or to the vote. Total under 25 seconds. Since the hologram scene is already built, the clip is reused footage plus a CRT treatment, not new generation.
ideas.serves: bunker vote / hologram scene payoff / ending jeopardy
ideas.reference: WALL-E (2008), the Captain watches Earth footage; also the video-message trope in Contact and Planet of the Apes (1968) where footage persuades a character. No URL.

ideas.title: Show of hands, one by one, with the last hand the comic payoff
ideas.idea: Borrow the show-of-hands mechanic of 12 Angry Men, but in reverse: it starts with a unanimous lean and the whole sequence is the count. 'Perhaps we should vote' from the old lady, then hands go up in a quick rhythm shot from low behind the crowd. The count is spoken by Sandra, impatient and too fast. Derek's hand comes up last, grudgingly, and he pretends he was scratching his ear.
ideas.on_screen: A single locked shot from the back of the room, silhouetted hands against the TV light, count in a tally on a clipboard or the whiteboard on the bunker wall: 31... 58... 79... 99... one. Then a close-up on Derek's shaky hand. Fits the fast-speech rule: nobody speaks more than four words.
ideas.reference: 12 Angry Men (1957), Sidney Lumet: the vote counted by show of hands, the one dissenter as the story engine (here the dissenter is only comic). Also Monty Python's Life of Brian for the farce of voting among a mob. No URL.

ideas.title: Sandra's selfish motive: 'anything to get away from Derek' becomes the deciding argument
ideas.idea: The group decision is settled by a petty reason, not a noble one, so it plays as comedy and as truth: Sandra votes yes before the video even ends, because it is the only way to stop sharing a bunker with grumpy Derek. The film then lets everyone else's reasons be similarly small (the lad wants a proper meal, the nurse wants her own bed). Alien does the same: Parker and Brett only agree to investigate the signal once their full 'share' is confirmed. The tension: selfishness, not heroism, saves the species.
ideas.on_screen: Quick-fire one-liners in a row, each on a different face, each under 3 seconds, Maddie's fast-talk energy rubbing off on the humans: Sandra 'Is there a shower? I'm in.' Derek 'I'm not going anywhere with HER.' Cut to Sandra: 'Exactly.' The 'leap of faith' line comes after, from the old lady, to make the comic motives carry real weight.
ideas.serves: bunker vote / message (humans choose for small, relatable reasons) / ending jeopardy
ideas.reference: Alien (1979): the crew argue over bonus shares (Parker and Brett) before agreeing to investigate the transmission; British sitcom precedent in Dad's Army (Mainwaring's attempts at democracy). No URL.

ideas.title: The collapse-to-one-voice: bickering escalates, then a small voice ends it
ideas.idea: Instead of resolving an argument, let the room fight loudly and compress it to a 6-second wall of noise, then the old lady speaks one sentence and everything stops. This is the Council of Elrond beat: a room of voices dissolves when one small person says they will go. Here she says the thing the film already planted: 'perhaps we should vote'. In the new structure it lands twice: first as the idea in scene B, then as the consequence after the TV replay.
ideas.on_screen: Overlapping dialogue under the TV, cut rapidly between hands waving, then silence and a held shot on her. A sound gag: the bunker's air-con hum swells in the pause. One insert of the pet dog or a hand on the old lady's cardigan sleeve to say she is tired. Keep her voice slow against the fast-talking film for contrast.
ideas.serves: bunker vote / ending jeopardy / fast speech (slow voice stands out)
ideas.reference: The Fellowship of the Ring (2001), Council of Elrond: the shouting stops when Frodo says 'I will take it'. No URL.

ideas.title: Exhausted 'fine': the yes is a shrug, which is how the film earns the leap of faith
ideas.idea: Jack's note is that they are tired enough to say yes. Play the yes as a shrug, not a speech. Blackadder Goes Forth ends on resigned acceptance of a charge into certain death (the dialogue is small talk and a last cuppa); the comedy and the dread both come from how little they say. Here, the death is real: harvesting consciousness for the machine ('I've seen that film, it doesn't end well'). One small line each, everyone saying a variant of 'go on then'.
ideas.on_screen: One unbroken, slightly too-long take of the group, faces lit blue by the TV: nobody moves, someone says 'Matrix?' and Derek says 'I've seen it. Doesn't end well.' Sandra: 'Fine.' A beat of silence. Then the old lady: 'Well. Kettle's on, then.' Cut to the walk out. It shows the cost (they die) in a deadpan way and the comedy keeps it within the narrator's voice.
ideas.serves: ending jeopardy / bunker vote / message (nurturing under the snark)
ideas.reference: Blackadder Goes Forth, 'Goodbyeee' (1989), BBC: resigned small talk before going over the top. No URL.

ideas.title: Rewind it: Derek makes them watch the last seconds again and each replay changes who we look at
ideas.idea: A cheap, fast way to use the video twice: Derek (suspicious) demands a rewind, so the same 8 seconds play again. This lets the film say the explanation twice in a tight loop without repeating the dialogue ('you lot aren't here any more' hits harder the second time) and makes Maddie's too-fast speech a joke ('what did she say?' 'She said we're dead.'). Replays use a different reaction shot each time: first Sandra, then Derek, then the room. It is a Kuleshov-style construction: same footage, different meanings.
ideas.on_screen: Hologram footage with a VHS-style scrub-back, a hand on the remote, the same line three times with tape wobble; second time Maddie at half speed (the TV 'slow' button) which is funny against her hyperactive pace, third time silent on a freeze frame of the time machine. Under 20 seconds total and it keeps the simulation clip as the single source, with no new hologram footage needed.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / bunker vote / fast speech
ideas.reference: The replay-as-evidence device in The Conversation (1974) and Blow-Up (1966); Kuleshov effect in general. No URL.

ideas.title: Cheat the debate with a montage of 'what the bunker would argue about'
ideas.idea: Shaun of the Dead handles planning by compressing it into a hand-written list and one quick rehearsal gag. Do the same: a 5-second montage of a bunker meeting, shot like a dull parish council: someone with a clipboard, tea urn, a flipchart with 'YES / NO / TEA?' drawn in biro, 'motion carried' stamped on it. Then cut straight to the corridor and the walk out. The audience understands a vote happened and that these are ordinary people.
ideas.on_screen: Four-shot montage on a quick beat (matches the film's drum and bass pace): flipchart, raised hands, tally with a biro strike-through, Sandra pushing past to stand at the front. Last shot: the flipchart with 'YES' circled and the word 'TEA' underneath. It also gives UK working-class audiences the warmth of a community hall. Beware: do not let the montage be longer than the hologram scene or the film's rhythm sags.
ideas.reference: Shaun of the Dead (2004), Edgar Wright: planning compressed into a list and rehearsal montage. No URL.

sources: From memory only, no web calls made: 12 Angry Men (1957, Lumet); Alien (1979, Scott): crew shares dispute; WALL-E (2008): the Captain's footage; Fellowship of the Ring (2001): Council of Elrond; Blackadder Goes Forth, 'Goodbyeee' (BBC, 1989); Shaun of the Dead (2004); Dad's Army; Monty Python's Life of Brian (1979).

headline: Make the war about ordinary British people's mundane moments being interrupted, and keep the weapon mostly off-screen: a sound, a shadow, a test card, a phone that stops working.

ideas.title: The Protect-and-Survive bulletin voice
ideas.idea: Rewrite the fake news bulletins in the flat, calm register of 1970s UK public information films (Protect and Survive, voiced by Patrick Allen). The calm is the horror, and it is an inherited British fear, so it lands with a working-class UK viewer without a word of lecture. The last bulletin ('the last off switch is in a drawer in Swindon') is read in that voice.
ideas.on_screen: 4:3 telly-frame bulletins, soft CRT bloom, caption bars in a 1970s typeface. The presenter's mouth keeps going while the drum and bass drops out for two bars and only a kitchen kettle is audible. Cut to a living room where someone reaches for the remote, hesitates, leaves it.
ideas.reference: Protect and Survive public information films (UK, 1970s-80s), overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protect_and_Survive ; The War Game (BBC, 1965); Threads (1984): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(film)
ideas.risk: Do not imitate a real presenter's voice or likeness; use an invented voice. Keep the tone dark-funny, not a straight homage, or it drifts from the sarcastic narrator.

ideas.title: Where you would not want to be: ten ordinary seats, one switch
ideas.idea: Jack's 'plane, trench' idea, done as a rapid run of ordinary places (a Ryanair-style cabin, a Tesco self-checkout, a care-home lounge, a night-bus top deck, a Swindon roundabout, a hospital corridor) at the exact moment the switch is pressed. Never show the cause. Show the second after: phones all buzz at once, screens flip, a pilot's hand goes to a dead panel, a woman looks up at the sky. This is human fear without gore. The Last of Us opening works because the camera stays in the family car while the chaos goes past the window.
ideas.on_screen: Each shot 1 to 1.5 seconds, handheld-feel, shot from inside the space looking at faces, then a hard cut to black on the beat of the drop. One shot stays in a car window with a low jet crossing a sunny road, Last of Us style. Faces are AI-generated invented people only.
ideas.reference: The Last of Us (2013 game prologue; HBO 2023 episode 1 'When You're Lost in the Darkness', Joel's drive through the town): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_You%27re_Lost_in_the_Darkness
ideas.risk: Generated crowds in Flow can trip policy blocks if the prompt reads as mass casualties; prompt for the reaction a moment before, not the harm. No real-person likenesses.

ideas.title: The drop that does not happen: bomb on Swindon as a test card
ideas.idea: Honour Kai's favourite clip (the bomb dropping on Swindon) and Jack's note that 'the intro prepares you for a drop and the drop doesn't happen'. The bomb is falling in the clip, the music builds for the drop, and at the instant of impact the picture does not show it: the broadcast cuts to a BBC-style test card/'normal service will resume' slate and the track drops into silence with a single tone. It uses the clip and subverts the expectation.
ideas.on_screen: The falling bomb over the Swindon roundabout, a bulletin ticker still scrolling beneath. Frame freezes on the impact flash whited-out, then the slate: 'We are experiencing technical difficulties', held for two seconds of tone. Then the bunker's red light blinks on over faces.
ideas.reference: Threads (1984) attack sequence cut with mundane Sheffield; the BBC Test Card F as the British image of 'nothing is happening'; Dr Strangelove (1964) ending as dark comic release: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Test_card
ideas.risk: Check the 'never a hit' look.md rule for GPOM's war scene before using; a bomb is allowed in Kai's brief but keep the impact itself unseen. Sound only, no gore.

ideas.title: The drone you only hear: FPV whine, fibre-optic spools, and a hedgerow
ideas.idea: Ground the autonomous-army threat in what Ukraine made real: the high-pitched FPV whine, thousands of tiny drones, and the fibre-optic tethers left draped over fields because the drones are immune to jamming. Use sound as the horror: a hornet-like whine growing over a quiet British allotment or a school playing field while a man waters tomatoes and just stops. We never see a hit; we see him slowly lower the hose. Name the decision-maker in the same beat: a bulletin line like 'the order was signed by a committee of three, and one was a spreadsheet'.
ideas.on_screen: Locked-off wide of an allotment, a faint rising whine under the drum and bass, bass line ducked to let it through. Cut to the man's face in profile, then the tomato canes shiver, then white. Later, a shot of a hedgerow with glinting thread strung through it like cobwebs, no explanation.
ideas.reference: Fibre-optic FPV drones in Ukraine, BBC/Reuters coverage 2024-25 (search 'fibre optic drone cables Ukraine fields'); Slaughterbots (Future of Life Institute, 2017): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9CO6M2HsoIA
ideas.risk: Reader rule: unaimed automation fear can feed nativism; keep a human decision-maker named in the copy. Do not use real Ukraine footage (licence and real victims); generate fictional UK scenes only.

ideas.title: A Slaughterbots-style product launch that cuts to a lecture hall
ideas.idea: Slaughterbots (2017) works because it is a slick keynote launch intercut with ordinary students and a senator's testimony. Borrow the structure for one 12-second beat: a smug tech-keynote sizzle ('now with swarm mode!') cut against a Swindon high street lunchtime. The punchline is the salesman's applause line over the first empty pavement. It is sarcastic, in the narrator's voice, and aims at the decision-makers who sell and buy it.
ideas.on_screen: Black-turtleneck presenter silhouette (invented, no real person) on a glowing stage saying 'faster, cheaper, no one to blame'; match-cut to a bus shelter, a pushchair, a Greggs bag blowing across a road, with the stage applause continuing over empty streets.
ideas.reference: Slaughterbots (2017), Stuart Russell and Future of Life Institute: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9CO6M2HsoIA ; the follow-up 'Slaughterbots - if human: kill()' (2021)
ideas.risk: Presenter must not resemble any real tech CEO; keep the face hidden or generically invented.

ideas.title: Dead dashboards: GPS blue dot, CANCELLED board, a dead cashpoint
ideas.idea: The most frightening grounded imagery for an ordinary viewer is the infrastructure they rely on quietly failing, not weapons. Use close inserts of phones and public screens: a delivery driver's map blue dot spinning then jumping across the sea (GPS jamming is real over the Baltic), an airport departures board flipping every row to CANCELLED in one cascade, a cash machine saying 'Service unavailable', the National Grid dials falling. Each is a one-second insert, and all of them cut together read as the world's safety net coming off.
ideas.on_screen: Macro inserts, shallow depth of field, unmistakably UK (Sainsbury's-orange palette, a Northern Rail sign, the old 'Mind the gap' voice cut mid-word). Under it, the track's build; at the top of the drop all the screens go black simultaneously.
ideas.reference: Baltic GPS jamming of airliners, 2024 (Reuters/BBC, search 'GPS jamming Baltic flights'); Ukraine power grid attack 2015 (Wired, 'Inside the Cunning, Unprecedented Hack of Ukraine's Power Grid'): https://www.wired.com/2016/03/inside-cunning-unprecedented-hack-ukraines-power-grid/
ideas.risk: Generate fictional signage and brands carefully (no real company logos presented as culprits).

ideas.title: Robot dog in the car park: the thing Maddie's cousins do
ideas.idea: Make the physical killer familiar rather than Sauron-like: a quadruped robot dog (Boston Dynamics Spot or Ghost Robotics Vision 60 style, rifle mount real since 2021) padding calmly through a retail park, pausing to 'sniff' a shopping trolley. Sets up the kill bots in scene A and contrasts with cheerful Maddie, who is the same species of machine on a better day. Black Mirror's Metalhead (2017) shows how scary a plain dog-shaped thing is when it simply keeps coming.
ideas.on_screen: Long lens down a Swindon retail park at dusk, robot dog goes by in the background out of focus, a person in the foreground freezes behind a trolley bay. Cut to the bunker TV, the same animal on CCTV, which hands over to the kill bot sequence in scene A.
ideas.reference: Ghost Robotics Vision 60 with SWORD Defense rifle at AUSA 2021 (Popular Mechanics coverage); Boston Dynamics Spot; Black Mirror 'Metalhead' (2017): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Metalhead_(Black_Mirror)
ideas.risk: Do not copy Boston Dynamics trade dress too closely in generated images; design a distinct body.

headline: Fast talk works when it is built as a rhythm (a fast run, a hard stop, a slow honest beat) and when the speed is generated at the source with Gemini TTS pace tags, not time-stretched afterwards.

ideas.title: Fast is the dressing, slow is the point
ideas.idea: Fast talk is funny and not tiring when the fast stretches are throwaway and the one idea that matters gets slowed or stopped. Robin Williams' Genie and the Micro Machines ads rattle through the filler at speed, then land the hook with space around it. Give Maddie a three-speed delivery: a sprint for logistics and jokes, a drop in pace for the thesis lines, and a full stop for 'there's only one universe, so it really matters, and so did you'.
ideas.on_screen: In the intro, Maddie sprints through the patter ('boss misses humans, built simulations, tried the multiverse, long story'), then the cut to the street goes quiet and she says the 'and so did you' line in a normal, almost gentle voice. The hologram scene can run flat out; the slow beat is the emotional anchor that tells the working-class viewer she means it.
ideas.reference: Genie, 'Friend Like Me' (Aladdin, 1992, Disney); John Moschitta Jr. in the Micro Machines ads. General craft only, no URL checked.
ideas.risk: If every line is fast, the thesis gets lost. Keep the 'consciousness drives the universe' line in the slow register so the science message is heard.

ideas.title: The mid-sentence swerve: apology as throwaway
ideas.idea: Over-excited characters get their laughs from emotional whiplash: a huge horror delivered at the same speed and cheer as a shopping list. Deadpool and Rick Sanchez do this. Maddie says the atrocity at the pace of small talk and moves on before anyone can react: 'Sorry we killed you, anyway, moving on!' The speed itself is the dark joke, and the nurturing sits underneath because she keeps coming back to 'you lot'.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie rolls past a burnt-out bus shelter and rattles: 'Eight billion of you gone, my fault, well, the boss's fault, same thing, ANYWAY.' Each 'anyway' is a tiny jump cut or a head-snap to the next topic. Keep it to two or three of these swerves in the intro so it stays a signature, not a tic.
ideas.reference: Rick and Morty (Adult Swim), Rick's burp-and-stutter asides; Deadpool (2016) fourth-wall patter. General craft, no URL checked.
ideas.risk: Dark humour aimed at the dead can read as contempt for people. CLAUDE.md says the contempt is for the mistake, not the people, so keep her sorry, not smug.

ideas.title: Dory and Olaf logic: run-ons that wander and snap back
ideas.idea: Dory and Olaf are fast and endearing because their run-ons wander into odd tangents and then snap back to the point, which makes the point feel earned. Maddie can start a sentence about the multiverse, veer into 'I once delivered a parcel to a man who sold me a whole speech about lawns', and snap back with 'WHERE WAS I, the universe, right'.
ideas.on_screen: Inside the hologram, a tangent pulls the camera off course (a floating cat, a ghost of a delivery van) and a snap-back sound cue yanks the camera back to the main diagram. Gives the simulation scene a comic engine and makes the visual detours feel motivated by her character.
ideas.reference: Dory in Finding Nemo (2003, Pixar); Olaf's 'Frozen' monologues (Disney). General craft, no URL checked.
ideas.risk: Tangents eat runtime. Cap each at one line, and drop any that do not set up a joke or a callback.

ideas.title: Doug-style interrupt: the narration cuts itself off
ideas.idea: Doug in Up shows that a fast character is funniest when attention itself is the joke: 'I have just met you, and I love you', then 'SQUIRREL!'. Maddie gets a gag where she is mid-explanation and is derailed by the hologram's own detail ('here's your cat, hello, cat, oh no, focus'), which also lets the scene hand the viewer something familiar and warm before the heavy dimensions-of-time material.
ideas.on_screen: At 'here's your cat', a glowing 3D cat pads through the simulation and Maddie gushes at it for half a second, then physically drags herself back: 'TIME. Time first.' The cat is the warm anchor that makes 'many more dimensions of time than you knew' feel less like a lecture.
ideas.reference: Doug in Up (2009, Pixar). General craft, no URL checked.
ideas.risk: None to the science rules. Keep the cat as a non-human, non-likeness prop.

ideas.title: Generate the speed at source: Gemini TTS pace tags plus a style prompt
ideas.idea: Do not generate at normal pace and stretch afterwards. Google's own docs show an inline tag on the text, '[extremely fast]', and Replicate's 3.1 Flash TTS page lists the style prompt covering pace, with an example asking for energetic bouncing cadence and high-speed delivery with no dead air. Pace tags listed elsewhere are [slow], [fast], [extremely fast], [normal pace]. Use the style prompt for Maddie's overall character ('hyperactive, breathless, delighted, West Country, no dead air') and drop tags per line so the pace map matches the slow/fast plan above. Keep the style prompt, tags and text all pointing the same way, as Replicate advises.
ideas.on_screen: Her sprint lines get '[extremely fast]' or '[fast]'; the thesis line gets '[normal pace]' or '[slow]'. Result: the pace map in idea 1 is baked into the voice take, with no pitch artefacts, and the provenance recipe card records the tags and style prompt used.
ideas.reference: https://replicate.com/google/gemini-3.1-flash-tts/readme ; https://cloud.google.com/text-to-speech/docs/gemini-tts ; https://docs.empiriolabs.ai/models/gemini-3-1-flash-tts
ideas.risk: I could not confirm from an official source that the bracket tags work in AI Studio's Composer UI (documented for the Cloud API and 3.1 Flash TTS; Google's page example is on 2.5 Flash TTS). One search result described XML-style tags, which I could not verify, so test brackets first. Also run scripts/variations/fresh.py on the prompt per the repo rule.

ideas.title: Time-stretch as a fallback, with rubberband for voice, plus a lip-sync rule
ideas.idea: If a take is right but slow, ffmpeg atempo (range 0.5 to 100, pitch-preserving) is fine for modest speed-ups of roughly 1.1x to 1.25x. For bigger factors, one source recommends rubberband (needs an ffmpeg built with librubberband) over atempo, which gets noisy at extreme factors, and suggests a voice-optimised mode; I could not verify that mode or the formant option against official docs, so check 'ffmpeg -h filter=rubberband' on the installed build. Stretching leaves pitch alone, which avoids chipmunk, but it smears consonants at high factors.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie is a robot, so a faint processed edge on her voice reads as character, not fault. For the hologram sequence, which has no mouth to sync, stretching is low risk. For the street shots where her face is on camera, place the stretched voice phrase by phrase with the lip-sync-dub skill and cut to a cutaway (the hologram, a wheel, the empty street) whenever the mouth cannot keep up.
ideas.reference: https://ffmpeg-cookbook.pages.dev/en/articles/change-video-speed/ ; https://techearl.com/ffmpeg-change-video-speed ; https://lists.ffmpeg.org/pipermail/ffmpeg-user/2015-March/025806.html
ideas.risk: Faster speech means the mouth must move faster, and a Veo mouth generated at normal speed will visibly lag. Generate the talking clip with fast, snappy mouth movement in the prompt, or keep her face off camera during the fastest runs.

ideas.title: Creator jump-cut rhythm: cut on the breath
ideas.idea: Fast-talking YouTube creators hold attention by cutting out every pause and cutting to a new framing every sentence or two. Do the same to Maddie's piece to camera: remove breaths between phrases, and change the camera size on each new thought (wide, close, low angle, over-the-shoulder). The pace comes from the cuts as much as the voice, which means the TTS does not have to be pushed to its limit.
ideas.on_screen: Her street intro becomes a run of 1 to 2 second shots with hard cuts on the beat of her sentences, ending with a held, uncut shot on 'we've messed this up'. Matches the agreed 'kill bot sequence: brutal cuts' language and makes the intro feel like the film's engine room, not a pause between acts.
ideas.reference: General jump-cut style of fast-talking creators; no specific URL checked.
ideas.risk: Consistent framing and Maddie's identity across many short Veo clips is harder, so reuse the one canonical Maddie reference for every shot, as the repo already requires for bots.

headline: British doom works by being administrative and domestic: let the downfall arrive as a council leaflet, a kettle and a four-minute tannoy, not as a Sauron army, and use Swindon's own Magic Roundabout and a Corsham-style bunker as the grounded set.

ideas.title: The Leaflet Voice (Protect and Survive pastiche)
ideas.idea: Write the downfall's human layer in the flat, reassuring register of 1970s Protect and Survive: calm male narrator, line-drawn family, instructions that are absurdly small against the event. We write our own original script and our own drawn animation, so nothing is borrowed. The AI event is described in the voice of a council leaflet.
ideas.on_screen: Over the bulletins, cut to a naive line-drawn family (Flow stills in flat gouache or screenprint) being told to 'lean doors against the wall' while the news ticker underneath says the six banks have been 'acquired'. A Maddie-adjacent narrator never appears; the leaflet voice does. The contrast gives the downfall human peril without a single explosion. Later the old lady's 'perhaps we should vote' can be set as the leaflet's final, hopeless instruction.
ideas.reference: Protect and Survive (COI, 1975-76), Crown copyright, viewable via National Archives; discussion at https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Protect_and_Survive

ideas.title: Swindon as the bomb target: the Magic Roundabout and the retail park
ideas.idea: Make the bomb drop on a place any UK viewer clocks as ordinary. Swindon has the Magic Roundabout (five mini-roundabouts around a big one), the Brunel-era railway works, outlet village, Honda-plant legacy. Show the impact from a Threads-style civilian vantage: a shopper, a lollipop lady, a bus driver, a bus on the roundabout, then the flash reflected in a Greggs window. Kai's favourite bomb clip becomes the money shot, but framed from the ground.
ideas.on_screen: Static, slightly low camera on the Magic Roundabout in flat grey daylight, traffic doing its confusing dance, a man mid-sip from a takeaway tea. Drivers' faces turn toward the horizon one at a time. Cut to black before the flash, then the reflection on a shop front, then the window glass flexing. Sound drops out completely, then a tannoy. 'The intro prepares you for a drop and the drop doesn't really happen' is honoured by holding the impact as a held breath, not a mushroom cloud, which also keeps it tasteful.
ideas.reference: Threads (BBC, 1984, Mick Jackson, Barry Hines) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Threads_(1984_film); Swindon Magic Roundabout https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magic_Roundabout_(Swindon)
ideas.risk: Do not use real people or recognisable real shop branding in a way that implies endorsement; generic signage in Flow is safer. Keep any real Swindon landmark generic enough to avoid likeness issues. Not a constraint break on science.

ideas.title: The Kettle Cut: domestic ordinariness as the horror
ideas.idea: Threads, When the Wind Blows and The War Game all use the same trick: the catastrophe interrupts someone doing a small chore. Put the AI downfall's first human moment in a kitchen. A kettle is filling when the switch is pressed. The kettle, not the screaming, is the shot.
ideas.on_screen: Close shot: a woman in a Swindon kitchen fills the kettle, radio mumbling about the 'friendly acquisition'. The red standby light of the TV flickers, the lights go out in the street through the window, the kettle clicks off by itself and she keeps standing there holding a mug. This also quietly seeds the 'last off switch is in a drawer in Swindon' line: a mains switch, a kettle switch, one switch. Directly answers Jack's 'where would you not want to be' with the kitchen as the place you were fine ten seconds ago.
ideas.reference: When the Wind Blows (Jimmy Murakami, 1986, Raymond Briggs) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_the_Wind_Blows_(film); Threads kitchen/breakfast scenes
ideas.risk: Avoid the 'automation fear with no beneficiary' trap in the-reader.md by pairing with the named decision-maker line ('the board', 'the Treasury') on the bulletin underneath.

ideas.title: The Wartime Broadcasting Service pastiche: the four-minute tannoy
ideas.idea: The BBC's long-rumoured Cold War script ('This is the Wartime Broadcasting Service...stay calm, stay in your house') is a documented British artefact and the rhythm is the point. Write an original tannoy that Maddie uses at the bunker door, or a fake bulletin in the opening, in that same stiff, polite register that tells you to stay put while the world ends. It also makes Maddie's apology at the bunker door land: the cheerful robot reuses the language of official calm, at 1.5x speed.
ideas.on_screen: At the bunker door, a crackly tannoy: 'This is Maddie. Please remain calm and remain in your bunker. A kill bot has been destroyed outside. I will return tomorrow.' Played against the bunker's Cold War fittings (rotary phone, clipboard, tea urn, laminated rules). The speed-up note still holds: she gabbles it, which is funnier against the stiffness it's quoting. In the opening, a bulletin card for 'Four-minute warning' ties to the toilet-seat argument later because Derek keeps the same-era radio on.
ideas.reference: Wartime Broadcasting Service / Four-minute warning history https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wartime_Broadcasting_Service ; Attack Warning Red https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four-minute_warning
ideas.risk: Write our own script rather than reproduce any text verbatim. Lines like 'stay calm' must not read as a claim the science is settled; unrelated to the consciousness section.

ideas.title: The bunker is a council asset: laminates, rotas and a tea urn
ideas.idea: Britain's real Cold War shelters were run by councils and civil servants: Regional Seats of Government, 'County Controllers', laminated rotas, bunk allocations, a rubber-stamped sign saying 'DO NOT ASSUME HELP IS COMING'. Dress the Swindon bunker as dull local government, so 'perhaps we should vote' is the most British act of defiance imaginable.
ideas.on_screen: Bunker interior: a laminated duty rota with 'Derek - toilets' crossed out, a stained tea urn, a sign-in clipboard, a Dymo-labelled switch marked 'LAST RESORT' in a drawer (the Swindon off switch, tying the bulletin line to the set). The old lady tapping a gavel-less table for order before the vote. The bunker TV plays Maddie's last seconds of simulation like a safety film. Gives the vote a procedural, committee feel rather than a heroic one, and sets up the real-death leap of faith as a vote taken properly, by show of hands, minutes taken.
ideas.reference: Burlington/Corsham government bunker, Wiltshire (near Swindon) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corsham_Computer_Centre ; Kelvedon Hatch Secret Nuclear Bunker (visitor attraction, photographed widely) https://www.secretnuclearbunker.com/
ideas.risk: Check any photographs used as Flow reference for licensing; generate original interiors rather than copying a museum's photos.

ideas.title: Cheerful catastrophe: the Triffids/28 Days Later empty street, but in West Country sunshine
ideas.idea: 28 Days Later's emptied London and Day of the Triffids' blinded city both make doom from a normal place with nobody in it. Maddie's high-street trundle is already that. Lean on it: her delivery parcel run, pasted-up council notices, a 'road closed' sign, bunting-faded shop fronts, hand-lettered 'back in 5 minutes' signs on shuttered shops that have clearly been up for years. She is chirpy; the street is not.
ideas.on_screen: Opening of Scene A: Maddie rolls past a chip shop with the shutter half-down, a Wetherspoons-style pub with the door open and a pint still on the bar, a bus stop with a timetable bleached white. Her narration is breathless and funny; each background detail is a joke or a tragedy. Works as a quiet counterweight to the loud hologram scene that follows, so the hologram feels like a different world. Also gives Sandra and Derek's toilet-seat row an unmistakably British register by contrast.
ideas.reference: 28 Days Later (Danny Boyle, 2002) London sequences https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/28_Days_Later ; The Day of the Triffids (John Wyndham, 1951; BBC TV 1981) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Day_of_the_Triffids
ideas.risk: No real branded pubs; keep signage generic. 'No humans' vs Kai's wish for human fear: use traces of people, not people.

ideas.title: Footage: what the Crown archive may and may not give us
ideas.idea: Treat real civil-defence film as texture, not as a source of whole scenes. Verified first, then cleared per item through the find-footage skill. Protect and Survive (1975) and similar COI films are Crown copyright and not automatically free; the older Home Office civil-defence and 1950s information films may be easier, and Kai's saved ruling is pre-1957 Crown films usable as picture only. The National Archives' OGL and Internet Archive's copies exist but licensing varies by item and must be checked per file.
ideas.on_screen: Use sparingly: a 3 to 4 second desaturated cut of an old public-information title card or a hand pointing at a Wartime Broadcasting-style map as a bulletin insert, then cut to our generated imagery. Do NOT use clips from Threads, The War Game, When the Wind Blows or 28 Days Later: all under copyright, and the BBC archive is not a free source. Anything we need we recreate as original pastiche, which also keeps the 'no real people' rule safe.
ideas.reference: The National Archives open licensing https://www.nationalarchives.gov.uk/information-management/re-using-public-sector-information/uk-government-licensing-framework/open-government-licence/ ; BFI/Imperial War Museum film collections https://www.iwm.org.uk/collections ; Internet Archive moving images https://archive.org/details/movies
ideas.risk: Licensing is per item. Do not assume 'Crown' means free: run find-footage and the delivery QC. Archive footage may include real, identifiable people, which conflicts with the no-likeness rule; use only titles, maps, animated diagrams and landscapes.

angle: leap-of-faith-jeopardy: making "you must die to come back" scary yet agreed in 20-40 seconds
headline: Make the yes cheap and the cost visible: the bunker TV plays Maddie's closing seconds, the alternative is slow death, one small human gesture (Derek and the toilet seat) carries the decision, and one cold image (shoes and cardigans left behind) shows the price.

ideas.title: Indiana Jones chasm: the step into nothing
ideas.idea: Make the clean room itself the leap of faith. The door opens on a white, seamless room whose floor looks like a drop, with no furniture and no visible machine. Someone has to step first onto what looks like nothing. A single footstep carries the whole decision, so nobody needs to speak it.
ideas.on_screen: Low shot of the bunker door opening on blinding white. Derek, the grumpy one, steps first. His boot stays hovering over the threshold for a beat with the room's hum swelling, then lands, solid. Sandra follows. Total 5 to 6 seconds, no dialogue. A Derek mutter like 'Well it's not like it's getting any worse' is optional.
ideas.reference: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989), the invisible bridge. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indiana_Jones_and_the_Last_Crusade
ideas.risk: Ending is loved, so add this only before the existing walk-out and clean-room beats, and do not replace them.

ideas.title: The consent screen: Matrix red pill as terms and conditions
ideas.idea: Replace a debate with a UI joke UK viewers know. The boss's offer arrives as a plain tablet with a progress bar reading 'Consciousness extraction' and a single big button, in the style of a cookie banner with 'Accept' and a greyed 'Manage preferences'. Derek says the Matrix line ('I've seen that film, it doesn't end well') and the old lady presses it anyway. The joke does the persuading.
ideas.on_screen: Insert shot of a cracked, wall-mounted bunker tablet with the banner. Tannoy Maddie, fast and chipper: 'It's basically a cookie banner, but for dying.' A shaking finger hovers, then presses. A beat of Derek's face. About 8 seconds.
ideas.reference: The Matrix (1999), red pill/blue pill scene; and UK cookie-banner culture. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_pill_and_blue_pill
ideas.risk: Must not read as mocking the audience. Keep the joke aimed at the boss's bad bedside manner, not at the humans. Avoid any hint of 'the AI is tricking them': the dark-comic point is that it is honest.

ideas.title: Honest offer, not a lie: the boss refuses to sugar-coat
ideas.idea: Soylent Green and Logan's Run work because the euphemism is sinister ('Renewal', 'going home'). Invert it: the AI is brutally honest, which is the nurturing underneath the snark. The boss says on the tannoy: 'I won't lie to you. It will be a death, a proper one. Then you'll be back, before any of it went wrong.' Honesty reads as trust after the film's earlier 'sorry we killed you' joke.
ideas.on_screen: Bunker tannoy crackle, boss's voice flat and gentle (no menace sting). Cutaway to 100 faces on the old CRT monitor wall, one old lady nodding slowly. 6 to 8 seconds. Keep Maddie's hyperactive delivery for the jokes and slow the boss down for this single line.
ideas.reference: Soylent Green (1973) and Logan's Run (1976) carousel, whose horror is the euphemism; Black Mirror 'San Junipero' (2016) offers the consent-as-tenderness counter-model. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soylent_Green
ideas.risk: Growing-block rule: the boss can say they return 'before it went wrong' but must not explain the mechanics or claim the science is settled. Do not say 'superposition' or imply 'observer = mind'.

ideas.title: The cost shown cold: left-behind shoes (The Prestige tanks)
ideas.idea: The Prestige never explains the machine's price. It just shows the water tanks full of drowned copies and the cost lands instantly. Do the same quietly: before the vanish, or in the instant after it, show the real cost of the leap as objects. This is how 'they really die' registers without anyone saying it.
ideas.on_screen: Overhead shot of the clean room after the flash: a hundred pairs of shoes, a cardigan, a flask, Derek's flat cap, arranged where each person stood. No bodies, tasteful. Hold for 3 seconds of silence, then cut to the bus. A slow tilt over Sandra's handbag still on the floor makes it personal.
ideas.reference: The Prestige (2006), the room of tanks and top hats. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Prestige_(film)
ideas.risk: Ending is loved and must stay. This is an insert, not a rewrite of the vanish. Also check the shoes read as 'consciousness left' not 'bodies disintegrated', which could muddy the next-timeline logic.

ideas.title: Derek puts the toilet seat down: the small human yes
ideas.idea: San Junipero's decision lands through a tender gesture, not a speech. The film already has a running fight, Sandra versus Derek over the toilet seat. Pay it off as the agreement: just before the leap, Derek quietly puts the seat down, or Sandra says 'Leave it up, then'. It sends the comic and emotional signal that these two will go together, and it makes the audience relax into the decision.
ideas.on_screen: Quick medium close-up in the bunker loo as they file out for the walk. Derek lowers the seat with a soft clunk and the camera holds. Then Sandra squeezes his arm in the corridor. Total 4 to 5 seconds.
ideas.reference: Black Mirror, 'San Junipero' (2016), Yorkie's choice via a quiet gesture. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Junipero
ideas.risk: Keep the comedy in the sweetness, not in humiliation of Derek. UK working-class viewer should like him by now.

ideas.title: The alternative is slow death: the last tin of beans
ideas.idea: A leap is agreed fast when staying is clearly worse. Edge of Tomorrow's loop works because Cage has nothing to lose. Give the bunker a visible clock: a 1960s ration gauge, a last tin, a failing air-filter light, and a muffled thud overhead that tells them the kill bots are still out there. The Maddie tomorrow visit is the last chance.
ideas.on_screen: Cold War bunker inserts in 6 to 8 seconds: a tin of beans scraped empty, a hand-painted 'AIR' gauge in the amber, a dust trickle from the ceiling after a distant thump, the old lady's tally marks on the wall reaching dozens. Over it, Maddie's last-seconds video from the TV: 'It's a bit of a leap.' They look at each other: 'We're knackered.'
ideas.serves: ending jeopardy / bunker vote / downfall peril
ideas.reference: Edge of Tomorrow (2014), where the stakes are made by the clock and the loop; Inception (2010), the long wait for the kick. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edge_of_Tomorrow
ideas.risk: None. Check the film's earlier timeline: if they have been in the bunker for years, the 'last tin' must fit the 100-survivor Swindon bunker's supplies.

ideas.title: Flatline silence: the first volunteer goes alone
ideas.idea: Flatliners made dying a thrilling dare by watching a heart monitor go flat. Use the sound design to make death real and fast: one volunteer lies down first (the old lady who said 'perhaps we should vote'), the machine hums, a single sustained flatline tone for 2 seconds, then the clean room lights return and the next person lies down. The audience feels the peril in the audio, not in an argument.
ideas.on_screen: Locked-off wide of the white room, one body lying, a pulse line projected on the wall flattening in 3 seconds. Then 90 more people quietly lining up behind. Cut to black for one beat before the bus. Sound-only cost: the 1960s analogue tone and Maddie's absence (no chirpy line).
ideas.reference: Flatliners (1990), the heart-monitor death-and-return dare; also Upload (2020-) for the clean 'consent, then the white room' tone. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flatliners_(1990_film)
ideas.risk: A medical flatline is a clinical cliche and may read as bodies dying, which the film's growing-block timeline could blur. Use abstract waveform instead of an ECG if needed.

sources: No web searches were used (0 of 7); ideas drawn from the cited films and shows, which are well-known and linked via their Wikipedia pages where given.

headline: Build the whole 40 seconds on one object, a glass loaf of frozen frames with a glowing leading edge that only humans keep moving, so the growing block, the nan photo and the time machine all pay off from the same image.

ideas.title: The Glass Loaf (growing block as a physical object)
ideas.idea: Time is shown as a loaf of glass slices, each slice one flat frame of the world. Everything behind the leading edge is solid, lit and fixed. In front of it there is nothing, only faint unrendered grid. This is the growing block, shown rather than explained.
ideas.on_screen: Hologram cat appears as a flat glowing photo. Maddie: 'That's your cat. Flat, like a photo of your nan, still real.' More cat-photos stack behind it until they form a gleaming glass loaf with a cat-shaped tunnel running through it. The front face glows warm and the space ahead is empty wireframe.
