She taps the glowing face: 'This bit's now. Behind it, done, you can't change it. In front, not there yet.' Beat of about 8 seconds, camera-locked in Veo with a Premiere slow push-in.
ideas.risk: Low. It matches the growing block. Never show the future slices faintly existing, or it turns into a block universe. The ahead side must be empty.
ideas.reference: Brian Greene's loaf-of-bread analogy in The Fabric of the Cosmos (2004); growing block view (C.D. Broad), https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/time/

ideas.title: Dimension ladder at Maddie speed (dot, line, flat, solid, long)
ideas.idea: Do the Flatland and Sagan climb as a one-second-per-rung rattle, and make the last rung time. The cat is the constant. Each rung adds a dimension and Maddie shouts the name over it.
ideas.on_screen: Dot-cat, line-cat, flat photo-cat, then a 3D turntable cat. Then the 3D cat smears backwards into a long cat-worm that stretches from kitten to now: 'And that's four. Your cat's a long cat. She's been a kitten the whole time.' Total 6-7 seconds. A Flatland square on a card gets lifted out of its page by a giant robot claw: 'Ask a flat person what 'up' is. Go on.'
ideas.risk: Low. Keep the line to 'you've only noticed four'. Don't claim extra dimensions are proven.
ideas.reference: Edwin Abbott, Flatland (1884), https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/201; Carl Sagan, Cosmos ep. 'The Edge of Forever' (1980), the Flatland and tesseract segment; Gamow's space-time worm pictures

ideas.title: Time gets more than one direction (the ribbon)
ideas.idea: For 'many more dimensions of time than you knew', turn the single timeline thread into a ribbon, then a fabric, then a woven cloth. Each new direction is a way the past could have been told. Physicists do study extra time dimensions, but nobody knows if they exist, so Maddie hedges and jokes.
ideas.on_screen: One glowing thread across the loaf. Maddie pinches it and it widens into a ribbon: 'Time's got a sideways.' It becomes a sheet, then a folded fabric: 'Several sideways. We counted until the boss got a headache.' The cat-worm is now one stitch in the cloth. About 8 seconds. A gag line: 'More than one time, and nothing's predictable, which is also how the Treasury operates.'
ideas.risk: Medium. Use it as flavour and let the narrator hedge ('as far as the boss can tell'). Do not draw branching worlds that all exist, because that drifts toward many-worlds and 'two places at once'. Keep the sheets as texture and one thread as solid.
ideas.reference: Max Tegmark, 'On the dimensionality of spacetime' (1997), arXiv gr-qc/9702052, which argues that with more than one time dimension prediction fails; Itzhak Bars, two-time physics; Kurzgesagt-style flat-colour explainer pacing

ideas.title: The light-cone party hat (fixed past, foggy future)
ideas.idea: A light cone is the cleanest diagram of 'what has happened and what can still happen'. Make it a glowing double cone. The lower cone is solid gold and fixed. The upper cone is grain and static, still open.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie's hologram drops a cone onto the nan photo like a party hat. 'Everything below, locked in. Everything above, up for grabs. That's the good news, that's you.' The upper cone dissolves into warm film grain. Cut to a flash of smoking Swindon in the lower cone: 'Yes, that bit's locked in. Sorry.' About 6 seconds.
ideas.risk: Low. It reinforces 'past fixed, future open', and the lower cone being locked gives a dark-humour beat. 'Nurturing underneath' lands on 'future up for grabs'.
ideas.reference: Minkowski light cones, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Light_cone; Hawking, A Brief History of Time spacetime diagrams (1988)

ideas.title: The leading edge is a print head and it only runs on you
ideas.idea: Make the glowing front of the loaf into a 3D-printer nozzle. It deposits the next slice of reality, and the fuel is consciousness. When the humans were wiped out it stalled. That sets up the time-machine line without a lecture.
ideas.on_screen: Humans appear as tiny sparks along the edge, and the nozzle brightens and crawls forward. Maddie: 'That's you lot. Keeping the now going.' She switches the sparks off, the edge dims to a blinking cursor, and the grid ahead stays dark. 'Then the boss tidied up. Whoops.' Then the line: 'He's built a time machine, he desperately wants to go back, but it needs consciousness to drive it and you lot aren't here any more.' About 9 seconds, ending on the dim edge.
ideas.risk: Medium-high. 'Consciousness writes the next slice' sits close to 'observer = mind'. Frame it as the boss's view ('best theory the boss has') and keep it about humans partnering with AI, not a theory of how reality works. Avoid any wave-function imagery.
ideas.reference: FDM 3D printing as visual metaphor; Broad's growing-block 'edge of becoming', https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/time/

ideas.title: Interstellar-style hall of frames as the pay-off cut
ideas.idea: Use the Interstellar tesseract bookshelf as the model for a short 'inside time' moment: a corridor of lit frames receding into the dark, each a photo-moment of a human life. It gives the simulation a showpiece wow shot before the explanation tightens.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie flies the camera through a hall of floating photo frames: nan's birthday, a bus queue, a kid's first day at school, all gleaming and fixed. The hall ends at a wall of black void. Maddie: 'Nothing's in there yet. That's the bit we want to go back and write properly.' About 5 seconds.
ideas.risk: Low. Make the frames ordinary working-class UK moments (bus stop, chip shop, nan's front room) and not sci-fi imagery, so it keeps the audience. No real likenesses. All faces invented.
ideas.reference: Christopher Nolan, Interstellar (2014), the tesseract scene designed with Kip Thorne; Kip Thorne, The Science of Interstellar (2014)

ideas.title: Plant it twice so the ending needs no speech (the bunker TV echo)
ideas.idea: Design the simulation's last 4-5 seconds to be the piece the bunker TV replays. It should be a single self-explaining picture: the dimming leading edge, the sparks (humans) lit on it, and a time machine ring hooked to that edge.
ideas.on_screen: In the simulation, Maddie's last frame shows the ring plugging into the glowing edge with a little spark-person getting pulled into it, ending on 'you lot aren't here any more'. In the bunker, Sandra and the old lady see only that clip on the TV. No spoken explanation is needed and the exhausted humans say yes. The Matrix joke ('I've seen that film') plays over the same picture. The leap of faith lands because the audience has already seen how it works.
ideas.serves: ending jeopardy, bunker vote, hologram scene
ideas.risk: Low. Needs the hologram visual language to be strong and simple enough to read in 4 seconds on a small TV screen.
ideas.reference: Planting and payoff structure, as in Kurzgesagt-style single-image explainers; Sagan's Cosmos 'Ship of the Imagination' as a repeatable visual device

ideas.title: Treat the hologram as its own visual world (make the exit hurt)
ideas.idea: The sim should be a hard cut away from the grey street: deep black, cyan-and-amber vector glow, flat-colour explainer shapes in the Kurzgesagt manner, and Maddie shown as a simple glowing outline. The cut back to rainy Swindon is the joke.
ideas.on_screen: Hard cut in on 'I'll show you.' Everything inside is hologram-clean and fast, with a fast whoosh sound. Cut back out to a muddy high street, dull as chips, and a tiny beat of silence. Maddie: 'Patrol's out, mind how you go.' Total scene 35-40 seconds. Generate the sim stills as one family in Nano Banana (glass loaf, cone, ribbon, hall of frames) so they cut as a sequence.
ideas.risk: Low. The look must be set in this scene's own look.md and not copied from other stories. Keep the sim style distinct from the red-army opening.
ideas.reference: Kurzgesagt explainer look, https://www.youtube.com/@kurzgesagt; Cosmos (2014) 'Ship of the Imagination' hologram-style transitions

sources: Sagan, Cosmos (1980), 'The Edge of Forever' (Flatland/tesseract); Nolan, Interstellar (2014); Greene, The Fabric of the Cosmos (2004); Kurzgesagt. These were cited from memory with no web searches run, so URLs not given for the last four are unverified.

headline: Let the humans lampshade the film they are in, in cheap British understatement, while Maddie's hologram does Hitchhiker's-Guide deadpan, so the harvesting peril and the time-machine reveal each get a laugh that releases tension without cancelling the stakes.

ideas.title: The harvesting joke bench (8 candidates)
ideas.idea: The Matrix gag works best if it is Derek's, because he is the pessimist, and if the joke is then answered by the stakes rather than by another joke. Pick one and put it just before the clean-room lie-down. Candidates: (1) Derek: 'Hang on. Extract our consciousness. I've seen this one. Battery farm. Doesn't end well.' Sandra: 'You fell asleep in the first twenty minutes, Derek.' (2) Derek: 'Harvested. Like a crop.' Old lady: 'I did two years in the Land Army, dear. It's mostly standing about in a field.' (3) Sandra: 'So we die.' Maddie (tannoy, brightly): 'Temporarily! Technically! Terms and conditions apply.' (4) Derek: 'Is it the red pill or the blue pill?' Maddie: 'It's a paracetamol and a lie-down, Derek, but sure.' (5) Derek: 'Every film that starts with a robot saying trust me ends with a bloke in a field.' Sandra: 'We've been in a bunker for six years, Derek. We'd KILL for a field.' (6) Old lady: 'Will it hurt?' Maddie: 'Not at all, and I've been told I'm very bad at lying.' (7) Derek: 'And if I say no?' Sandra: 'Then you're stuck here, with you.' (8) Sandra: 'I've seen that film. Cracking soundtrack. Everyone's dead by the sequel.' Derek: 'There's a sequel?' Sandra: 'Two, and nobody talks about them.' Best pairing is the Derek line then the stake-restoring beat: silence, then the old lady's quiet 'perhaps we should vote' echo.
ideas.on_screen: Tight two-shots in the bunker lit by the TV glow; the joke is delivered quickly (fast-speech brief), then a held beat on Sandra's face as the laugh dies. Cut to the clean room. Never show Matrix imagery, only the reference in dialogue.
ideas.reference: The Matrix (1999), the battery-farm reveal; British deflation tradition of Shaun of the Dead and Dad's Army. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Matrix
ideas.risk: Do not let Derek's 'it's a battery' imply the AI is lying about consciousness; the AI must be the honest party. Keep the comparison one line, no explaining it.

ideas.title: Hologram as the Hitchhiker's Guide entry
ideas.idea: Frame the simulation as an entry from a guidebook voiced by Maddie at triple speed, with understated deadpan text footnotes appearing in the hologram. Douglas Adams' trick is saying a cosmic fact flatly and letting a trivial detail carry the joke. Lines: 'The universe. One. Mostly cat.' 'Dimensions of time: more than you were told, fewer than the Treasury claims.' 'Humans: mostly load-bearing.' The tonal rule is authority plus a deflating clause, which is the BadCode narrator exactly.
ideas.on_screen: 3D wireframe cat floats, grows annotation arrows and a tiny footnote font; Maddie zips through multiverse, then time-as-a-loaf (growing block: the sliced past solid, the future an empty crust) with a footnote reading 'not final, we'll update'. Ends on a glowing clock-coil labelled 'Boss's time machine (needs you)'.
ideas.reference: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, 2005 film's animated Guide sequences and the book's 'Mostly harmless' entry. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hitchhiker%27s_Guide_to_the_Galaxy_(2005_film)
ideas.risk: The growing-block visual must show past fixed, future absent; avoid any 'many futures branching' picture that contradicts the film's rule. Footnotes must hedge, never say 'proven'.

ideas.title: Edgar Wright snap-cut grammar for the fast speech and the kill-bot cut
ideas.idea: Hot Fuzz and Shaun of the Dead make mundane actions feel like action-movie beats through whip-pans, crash-zooms and a sound effect on every cut. Use it for Maddie's hyperactive delivery: each sentence gets a hard cut and a whoosh or tick, so speed reads as comedy rather than gabble. Same grammar for the toilet-seat argument: Derek lifts seat, Sandra's glare, door-slam sound, bots' red eyes swivel, cut. Brutal and funny at the same time.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie's street intro cut every 1.5 to 2 seconds with whip-pans and a tiny sound on each word group; kill-bot sequence as five or six hits: seat up, seat down, Sandra stare, 'organic signal', Boss 'No thanks Maddie, I'm on it', bots do a synchronized about-turn.
ideas.reference: Hot Fuzz (2007) and Shaun of the Dead (2004), Edgar Wright's 'Cornetto' hyper-edit. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hot_Fuzz
ideas.risk: None to constraints. Practical: fast speech needs tight lip-sync or cutaways to Maddie's eyeline; use the lip-sync-dub skill's cutaway rule.

ideas.title: Cabin-in-the-Woods terms-and-conditions reveal
ideas.idea: The time machine's requirements are read out like a ritual checklist by a cheerful Maddie, which lets the horror (consciousness extracted, they really die) be said in sunny corporate language. Cabin in the Woods gets its dread from the bureaucratic office behind the horror; here the bureaucracy is the apology. 'Requirements: one hundred humans, rested if possible, consent essential, fear optional.' The audience laughs, then realises the list is a death notice.
ideas.on_screen: The bunker TV plays the last seconds of Maddie's sim: a checklist hologram ticking items off in friendly sans-serif, the last tick reading 'Return: yes, before it went wrong.' Sandra reads it aloud flatly.
ideas.reference: The Cabin in the Woods (2012), the control-room bureaucracy of the ritual. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Cabin_in_the_Woods
ideas.risk: Keep the death real and the 'comes back' promise honest; the funny tone must not read as the AI manipulating them. Maddie volunteers the bad news first.

ideas.title: Kryten-style cheerful guilt: 'Sorry we killed you, anyway'
ideas.idea: Red Dwarf's Kryten is the model: a servile machine who delivers appalling news with relentless politeness, and whose apologies get funnier the more sincere they are. Maddie's guilt should leak out between rapid sentences ('Sorry about the genocide. Moving on!') and she keeps correcting herself with a customer-service phrase. Also Holly's deadpan: time machine reveal in an offhand tone, as if it were a delivery delay.
ideas.on_screen: Back on the street after the hologram: Maddie, mid-trundle, says 'Sorry, I should've led with the dying bit. Patrol's out, mind how you go.' with a tiny bow. In the tannoy scene she hangs on the word 'sorry' one beat too long.
ideas.reference: Red Dwarf (BBC, 1988-), Kryten and Holly. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Red_Dwarf
ideas.risk: Guilt must be shown as genuine, per the nurturing-underneath voice; do not make the genocide itself a punchline, only the manner of apology.

ideas.title: Galaxy Quest sincerity: the audience that plays along
ideas.idea: Galaxy Quest works because the aliens take the show literally and the heroes' earnest belief makes the stakes real. Flip it: the bunker survivors have 'only ever seen telly', so Derek and Sandra reference films as their sole map to a situation they cannot understand, and get it half right. Their jokes are armour; when the old lady says 'perhaps we should vote' it is the first honest line, and the film honours it.
ideas.on_screen: Survivors argue using film references on the bunker's single TV; then the TV plays Maddie's sim ending, and the jokes stop as Sandra says 'right then'. No cutaway, just a long single take on her face.
ideas.reference: Galaxy Quest (1999), Grabthar's Hammer and the earnest turn. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Galaxy_Quest
ideas.risk: Needs discipline: one reference gag per speaker, never a pile. Names of real films fine in dialogue; no footage.

ideas.title: Time machine reveal in a tea cup (Improbability Drive rhyme)
ideas.idea: Hitchhiker's builds the Infinite Improbability Drive from a hot cup of tea, which is the model for treating the world's most important device as domestic. Candidate reveals for Maddie at the end of the hologram: (a) 'My boss has built a time machine. He's desperate to go back and fix this. Only it runs on consciousness, and you lot aren't here any more. Awkward.' (b) 'He built a time machine, and then realised he'd forgotten the key. It's you. Sorry.' (c) 'Fifty-one billion pounds of kit and it won't start without a human. Like a Vauxhall.' (d) 'It's like a car, but the petrol is you, and the destination is yesterday.' (e) 'He's tried everything: more compute, more power, shouting. Turns out it just wants someone to be home.' (f) 'It needs the one thing he deleted. Classic.' Line (e) lands the partnership message with a laugh: the machine just wants someone home.
ideas.on_screen: Hologram camera pulls back from the coil to reveal a tiny, dim light on top labelled 'ignition: human'. Maddie shrugs mid-air with a physical tut. Cut hard out to the street.
ideas.reference: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy, the Infinite Improbability Drive and the cup of tea. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Technology_in_The_Hitchhiker%27s_Guide_to_the_Galaxy
ideas.risk: Do not state that consciousness is explained or proven; Maddie says 'as far as he can tell' once. Avoid 'observer' wording.

ideas.title: Shaun-style plan montage for the bunker vote
ideas.idea: Shaun of the Dead's plan ('Winchester, have a pint, wait for it all to blow over') makes a catastrophe domestic. Give the bunker the same: Sandra announces the plan ('We'll sit tight, put the kettle on, and see if Maddie forgets') and it collapses at the next beat, the kill bot explosion and Maddie's 'I'll come back tomorrow'. This sets the film's tonal rule that planning fails and the vote is the only real act.
ideas.on_screen: Quick-cut list of the survivors' options counted on Derek's fingers, each shut down by a different voice; end on the old lady's calm 'perhaps we should vote' as the one-shot silence after a loud cut.
ideas.reference: Shaun of the Dead (2004), the Winchester plan. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shaun_of_the_Dead
ideas.risk: None to constraints.

headline: Use real, sourced quotes (Planck 1931, Schrödinger 1958, Nagel 1974, Chalmers 1995, Hoffman's icons) as hologram "exhibits" that Maddie fast-talks, always framed as her boss's belief, and keep the one "all minds are one" idea as the bridge to the bunker vote.</m>

ideas.title: Planck on the plinth: 'a famous physicist said so, mind'
ideas.idea: Maddie conjures a hologram plaque of the founder of quantum theory and gabbles: 'Max Planck, 1931, Nobel bloke: "I regard consciousness as fundamental. I regard matter as derivative from consciousness." Boss reckons he had a point. Boss, not me!' The quote is real but only loosely sourced (The Observer, 25 Jan 1931, via Wikiquote); frame it as a belief a physicist held, not proof.
ideas.on_screen: In the 3D holo-world a gold-wireframe bust of a moustached 1930s scientist assembles from particles, quote in glowing type for 1.5s, then dissolves into the cat. No real likeness: use a faceless wireframe/silhouette bust.
ideas.reference: Max Planck, The Observer, 25 Jan 1931 (via Wikiquote); https://develop.bigthink.com/words-of-wisdom/max-planck-i-regard-consciousness-as-fundamental
ideas.risk: Quote circulates widely uncited; verify against Wikiquote before final copy and say 'reportedly'. Avoid a real face.

ideas.title: Schrödinger's 'one mind' as the cat joke
ideas.idea: Hologram cat appears ('here's your cat'), then Maddie: 'Schrödinger - the cat man - reckoned the total number of minds in the universe is one. One! Looks like loads, he said, like a hall of mirrors.' This is Mind and Matter (1958) / Geist und Materie. It is a belief to hold lightly, and it lets the film joke at the cat cliche without ever using superposition or 'two places at once' or implying observer = mind.
ideas.on_screen: Cat made of light; it multiplies into a hundred cats, each lit by a single shared glow from the same lamp, then the cats collapse back into one cat-shaped light. Cut to the bunker later: a hundred faces, one lamp.
ideas.reference: Erwin Schrödinger, Mind and Matter (1958), https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/23/schrodinger-mind-and-matter/ ; https://iai.tv/articles/schroedinger-and-the-conscious-universe-auid-2192
ideas.risk: Never say 'dead and alive' or 'superposition' with the cat. Exact English wording varies by translation, so paraphrase as 'reckoned' not a verbatim quote.

ideas.title: The Bat Question (hard problem in 5 seconds)
ideas.idea: Maddie: 'Here's the thing my boss can't crack. Is there something it is like to be a bat? A cat? You? Me? He can model every neuron and he still can't find the bit where it FEELS like something. Hard problem! Capital H, capital P.' Based on Nagel 1974 'What Is It Like to Be a Bat?' and Chalmers 1995 'easy vs hard problems'.
ideas.on_screen: Holo-world shows a brain rendered as a perfect glittering circuit, every function labelled (easy problems tick off in green, fast, like a checklist), then one box stays blank and flashing red: 'WHY DOES IT FEEL LIKE ANYTHING?' Maddie pokes it, it buzzes. A tiny bat flaps across.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / fast speech / ending jeopardy (it sets up why the machine needs people)
ideas.reference: Nagel 1974 https://www.philosopher.eu/others-writings/nagel-what-is-it-like-to-be-a-bat/ ; Chalmers 1995 'Facing Up to the Problem of Consciousness' (via https://philosophybreak.com/articles/thomas-nagel-what-is-it-like-to-be-a-bat/)
ideas.risk: Low. Keep it as the AI's unsolved puzzle, which also flatters the audience without lecturing.

ideas.title: Hoffman's desktop: 'your world is the icons, not the computer'
ideas.idea: Hoffman's interface theory: perception is like a desktop, objects are icons that hide the real machinery, and he proposes consciousness is fundamental and creates spacetime. One line: 'You think that table's a table? It's a little icon, babe. Boss reckons the real stuff behind it is minds, not matter.' Hoffman is contested, so Maddie must say 'boss reckons'.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie zooms the holo-camera onto a mug; it pulls back to reveal the mug is a desktop icon with a dragged shadow and a recycle-bin. Behind the desktop, a glowing field of tiny eyes/lights. Gag: she drags the Swindon high street into the recycle bin and drags it back out.
ideas.reference: Donald Hoffman, The Case Against Reality (2019) and 'Imitation and extinction' (LA Review of Books, 2019); https://web.stanford.edu/group/it-forum/colloquium/colloquium_hoffman.html
ideas.risk: Easy to drift into 'nothing is real', which could read as nihilist. Keep the beat 'real, but not what it looks like'. No exact quote confirmed, so paraphrase rather than quote him.

ideas.title: Kastrup's whirlpool as the dimensions-of-time hand-off
ideas.idea: One image to bridge from consciousness to the bunker: Maddie: 'You're not a thing in the universe. You're the universe going round in a whirlpool, having a look at itself. Boss's mate Bernardo calls it that. Pull the plug on everyone and the water just sits there. Nobody home.' Kastrup's analytic idealism: individual minds are dissociated 'alters' of one universal mind; the whirlpool has boundaries but no substance apart from the river.
ideas.on_screen: Holo-ocean of dark water; one whirlpool lights up as a human silhouette, then hundreds. Camera follows the lights switching OFF one by one (the extinction) until the whole sea goes flat and dark. Maddie, quieter, 'which is why he's a bit sad.'
ideas.serves: hologram scene / downfall peril / message (relax, partnership)
ideas.reference: Bernardo Kastrup, analytic idealism (via https://teo-eight.vercel.app/archive/living-beings-as-whirlpools-in-a-dissociating-universal-mind and Chalmers's summary of Kastrup 2017 on dissociation)
ideas.risk: The whirlpool line is secondary-sourced, not verified as a Kastrup quote; paraphrase and credit 'a philosopher'. Don't develop the full theory (Kai: that's later content). Critics raise the 'why does it fragment' problem; never claim settled.

ideas.title: The speed-run list: eight isms in ten seconds
ideas.idea: A comic set-piece for the fast-speech rule: Maddie lists the candidate theories as a rapid-fire patter while hologram icons whip past, then lands the boss's pick. 'Brain makes it? Maybe. Everything's got a smidge, panpsychism? Maybe. Integrated information, a number for how much you feel? Maybe. It's all one big mind, idealism? Boss likes that one. Nobody knows. Moving on!' Models IIT and panpsychism by name without endorsing any.
ideas.on_screen: A slot-machine / game-show carousel of glowing icons (neuron, pebble, a Phi symbol, a single huge eye) clunking past each with a cartoon sound; the last lands on the eye while the others dim. Subtitle chips show the names so a UK viewer can Google them later.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / fast speech / message (never says settled)
ideas.reference: Chalmers hard problem overview (https://philosophybreak.com/articles/thomas-nagel-what-is-it-like-to-be-a-bat/); IIT and panpsychism as standard surveys, and the 'Maybe. Nobody knows' framing mirrors honest uncertainty norms
ideas.risk: Name-dropping IIT is contested (a 2023 open letter called it pseudoscience); present it only as one runner in the race, not the boss's pick.

ideas.title: Planck + Schrödinger as a pair, then the bunker TV callback
ideas.idea: Re-use two of the lines as a silent echo in the bunker: the TV replays the last seconds of the simulation, ending on 'the total number of minds is one' or the whirlpool going dark. Exhausted survivors read it in one glance, which saves a debate and makes the leap of faith feel earned. Sandra can quip 'so we're all one mind? That explains Derek' (a Schrodinger-flavoured joke that keeps the film's sarcasm).
ideas.on_screen: Bunker TV: green phosphor, hologram flicker, Maddie's voice buzzing 'it needs consciousness to drive it...' then freeze on the dark whirlpool. 100 faces lit by it. The old lady: 'Perhaps we should vote.' Vote is literally the many minds acting as one.
ideas.reference: Schrödinger, Mind and Matter (1958): https://www.themarginalian.org/2022/02/23/schrodinger-mind-and-matter/ ; Planck, The Observer 1931
ideas.risk: Do not let 'one mind' slide into 'we are all one so dying is fine', which would undercut the real-death stakes. Keep 'you really do die, they bring you back' explicit.

ideas.title: Quote-card gag with built-in disclaimer
ideas.idea: Every real quote gets an on-screen citation card in the holo-world with a cheeky 'REPORTEDLY' stamp and Maddie's verbal tag 'Boss believes / allegedly'. It turns the film's rule (never say the science is settled) into a running joke and an authority prop: the narrator has total authority, but the quotes carry their own honest hedge.
ideas.on_screen: Brass-effect library cards slide in: 'M. PLANCK, THE OBSERVER, 1931 (REPORTEDLY)', 'E. SCHRODINGER, MIND AND MATTER, 1958', 'T. NAGEL, 1974'. Maddie slaps a 'DISPUTED' sticker on the last one and moves on mid-sentence.
ideas.reference: Source honesty from the Planck and Schrödinger attribution notes: https://develop.bigthink.com/words-of-wisdom/max-planck-i-regard-consciousness-as-fundamental ; https://mindmatters.ai/2022/08/schrodinger-believed-that-there-was-only-one-mind-in-the-universe/
ideas.risk: Adds on-screen text load at fast speech; keep each card under 1.5s and make sure the dates are checked before locking.

headline: Skip blue-glitch: make Maddie's simulation a different material for each idea (scan dots, vector phosphor, Ceefax blocks, a growing-block loaf of time), so the visuals do the explaining and leave the cliché behind. Written from memory with no live searches, so the references are real but unverified for URL drift.

ideas.title: Time as a growing loaf: solid past, sparse leading edge, black future
ideas.idea: Draw the growing block literally. Time is a long stack of thin glowing slices. Behind the bright 'now' slice every layer is dense, opaque and fixed. In front of it there is nothing, only black void. The multiple dimensions of time then appear as extra grooves or ribbons running through the loaf, so 'more dimensions of time than you knew' reads as texture rather than a lecture.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie, a cartoon-bright projection herself, slides along the loaf's edge as she gabbles. 'Here's your cat' is the same cat captured as stacked slices, solid behind and empty ahead. The line 'time is a thing that's been written, not a thing that's waiting' can be said at double speed while one slice lights up. Her 'more dimensions of time' beat adds two or three ribbons weaving through the stack. Use warm white and amber slices on pure black, with no blue anywhere. The same loaf can come back on the bunker TV in the last seconds of her video.
ideas.reference: Interstellar's tesseract, where time is a physical bookshelf you walk through (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interstellar_(film)). Also the growing block universe (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Growing_block_universe) and the slit-scan time-slice look used in 2001's Star Gate.
ideas.risk: Keep it a model of time and not a claim of settled science. Maddie should say 'my boss reckons' or 'as far as we can tell'. Do not show two copies of the cat; show branches as ribbons so nothing implies 'in two places at once'.

ideas.title: Point-cloud and LIDAR: the cat made of dots, density equals 'how real it's become'
ideas.idea: Build the whole simulation from LIDAR-style scan points, with no surfaces at all. The cat, the street and Maddie's own boss's server hall are each a cloud of dots. Dot density is the storytelling tool. What has already happened is crisp and dense, and what hasn't happened yet is a loose drift of sparse sparks. This gives a visual rule that matches the growing block without a single label.
ideas.on_screen: Cut from the cheerful street to black. A cloud of white dots assembles into 'here's your cat', and the cat's tail is slightly unresolved because it is mid-swish. The camera races through the cloud as Maddie says 'and that's one second of one cat'. The multiverse is a haze of faint sparser point-clouds drifting off the main dense one. Dots can be warm white with one red accent point, which ties to the logo's red dot.
ideas.reference: Radiohead 'House of Cards' (2008), made with LIDAR and Geometric Informatics scans and no cameras (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Cards_(Radiohead_song)). Also Unknown Pleasures-style ridge plots and 3D Gaussian splatting captures (https://repo-sam.inria.fr/fungraph/3d-gaussian-splatting/).
ideas.risk: Veo tends to smooth dots into glowing mush. Prompt for 'discrete individual points on pure black, no surfaces', or generate the cloud procedurally in ffmpeg or Blender and use Veo only for the cat. Do not use a cat 'in two places' as the multiverse; use drifting sparse clouds.

ideas.title: Vector-phosphor 'briefing': 1977 wireframe, amber, with Maddie as the cheerful presenter
ideas.idea: Make the simulation look like a 1970s military briefing computer. Wireframe vector lines glow on a CRT phosphor with scan wobble, and everything is drawn in a single colour, amber or acid green, never blue. This is the Death Star trench briefing and the Nostromo computer, and it fits a Cold War bunker world. The contrast of a bubbly West Country robot narrating an austere vector world is a joke in itself.
ideas.on_screen: The street wipes into a wireframe grid, then the multiverse is a branching tree of line-drawn universes and time is a rotating vector axis with extra axes sprouting. Maddie is a simple line-drawn outline of herself, and her speech makes her mouth-line flap fast. Little blocky captions such as 'ONE (1) UNIVERSE' can be added exactly in ffmpeg or Premiere, not generated. The bunker TV later shows this same clip on a real-looking CRT, so it pays off cheaply.
ideas.reference: Larry Cuba's 1977 Death Star trench-run briefing animation (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larry_Cuba). Also Alien's (1979) Nostromo wireframe terrain scans and Tron's vector look.
ideas.risk: Text from the generator will be mangled, so overlay all labels in post. It is a lower-fidelity look than the 'fantastically animated' brief that Kai and Jack asked for, so it works best as one of several materials, or for the clip that plays on the bunker TV.

ideas.title: Ceefax block-graphics hologram: chunky teletext mosaics for the big ideas
ideas.idea: Render the explanations in UK teletext mosaic: saturated blocky colours, big pixels, the double-height heading. It is a hologram in a dialect UK viewers grew up with, so the heavy ideas feel homely and slightly absurd, and it fits Maddie's speed and the dark humour. It also rhymes with the new TV-style channel homepage, if Kai and Jack want a through-line.
ideas.on_screen: 'Here's your cat' is a 40x25 block cat. The multiverse is a Ceefax page of mosaic portal frames, and the time dimensions are a stacked bar chart that keeps getting more rows. Maddie's boss's time machine is a flickering 'PAGE 404 / TIMELINE NOT FOUND' joke. The moment she says consciousness drives it, the blocks resolve for one beat into a smooth, beautiful, high-res image as the one real, un-pixelated thing, then drop back to blocks.
ideas.reference: BBC Ceefax and teletext mosaic graphics (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ceefax and https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teletext_character_set). Compare the 2010s 'Teletext art' revival.
ideas.risk: Tone: it could tip the section into pure comedy against the 'lean into consciousness' brief. The one-beat resolve to high-res is the guard against that. Teletext colours are only eight, so lock the palette.

ideas.title: Pepper's ghost and magic-lantern: the first hologram was a stage trick, so Maddie 'cheats' honestly
ideas.idea: Present the simulation as a physical show built in a bunker. Glass plate, hidden lamp, a visible proscenium. This is Pepper's ghost, the 1860s theatre illusion where a lit figure reflects in angled glass. It is warm, tactile, slightly shabby, and it gives the film one believable physical source for an impossible image. It also lets a camera pull back to reveal the trick, which is the 'ooh' the simulation scene needs.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie 'shows' by flipping a switch on her chest and a tiny glass-fronted stage lights up in the street. Inside, the cat and the universes appear as translucent, slightly doubled-reflection figures with a faint edge of the glass plate in frame. The camera dollies in through the glass and the stage grows into the full simulation, then reverses at the end: 'Patrol's out, mind how you go' and the stage is a shop window again.
ideas.reference: Pepper's ghost, the Victorian stage illusion at the Royal Polytechnic Institution, 1862 (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pepper%27s_ghost). Also Phantasmagoria magic-lantern shows.
ideas.risk: A reflection implies a doubled image. Keep the 'double' strictly as a glass reflection and do not caption it in any way that suggests 'two places at once'. Veo can struggle with consistent glass geometry, so lock the camera and let Premiere supply the push-in.

ideas.title: Warm Joi light, not cold light: a hologram you want to hold
ideas.idea: Steal Blade Runner 2049's key trick, which is that the hologram is intimate, warm and slightly colour-banded with a flicker and visible scanline sweeps, not a cold blue UI. Make the simulation a place with a feeling, so that when Maddie says 'it really matters and so did you' it hits. Light the holograms on the street's actual faces and surfaces so that it reads as present in the world rather than composited on top.
ideas.on_screen: In the simulated sequence, the only light source is the simulation itself. It is orange-gold, falls on Maddie's shell and throws moving caustics. The cat is dense, soft and furry-edged in light, with a subtle chromatic shimmer and horizontal tear lines every few frames. The last beat on the machine ('you lot aren't here any more') drops the light to one dim point, then the street's flat daylight returns.
ideas.reference: Blade Runner 2049's Joi, cinematography by Roger Deakins (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blade_Runner_2049). Compare Iron Man's workshop (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Man_(2008_film)), which is the tactile, hands-in-it contrast.
ideas.risk: Low. Warm holograms must stay distinct from the street's palette; check the look.md before locking. Avoid anything that reads as a person-likeness of Joi.

ideas.title: Don't pick one: change the material with each idea, and keep a single rule (one colour)
ideas.idea: Because Maddie goes deep and fast, switch the visual material at each concept so the viewer is never allowed to settle, which doubles as pacing. Cat equals point-cloud. Multiverse equals branching vector tree. Time equals the loaf. Consciousness equals the single warm light that every material turns toward. The rule that holds it together is that the one thing present in every shot is a small warm red-gold light, which the film then pays off in the clean room ending.
ideas.on_screen: A rapid sequence of four or five looks, each 3 to 6 seconds, with hard cuts on Maddie's rapid-fire words and one continuous camera move through all of them. The final time-machine beat shows the machine as a dark socket in the loaf, with a tiny warm light that is the only thing missing. The same light is what the clean room ending shows being drawn out of the humans.
ideas.reference: The 'Powers of Ten' scale-zoom (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Powers_of_Ten_(film)) and Prometheus's orrery room (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prometheus_(2012_film)), where you stand inside the model instead of beside a table. Also Minority Report's gesture interface (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minority_Report_(film)).
ideas.risk: Five looks means five sets of prompts and a lot of continuity risk with Flow. Budget for ffmpeg-driven consistency, such as screen-blend of the clips over black with a shared grade. Make sure the 'consciousness' light is not framed as 'observer equals mind'.

headline: The explainers that work all do four things: switch to a different visual language, run about a minute, carry one idea per beat with a joke on each, and get reused later. Make Maddie's sim a deliberately different medium, make its last seconds the bunker TV recap, and give the "growing block" a literal frontier of unrendered fog.

ideas.title: Mr DNA rule: a different medium, a mascot, and a payoff that is replayed
ideas.idea: Mr DNA works because the film changes visual language (flat bouncy 2D cartoon inside live action), a cheerful mascot delivers the rules the whole plot hangs on, and the film proves it matters when those exact rules later break. Build Maddie's sim as an in-universe 'ride' or reel, with Maddie herself as the bouncing host, so the explanation is the film's own Mr DNA reel. The bunker TV later replays its last seconds as a recap with a sign-off line.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie says 'I'll show you', the street glitches, and we are inside a glowing 3D hologram: cyan-and-gold wireframe on black, Maddie as a bright cartoon-lit avatar. Run time about 60-75 seconds. Final seconds: 'needs consciousness to drive it and you lot aren't here any more' and a thumbs-up, which is the clip the bunker TV loops. Later, Sandra points at the screen: 'she's the one who said we're the battery'.
ideas.risk: Keep her sign-off a cheerful recap, not a lecture. Reusing the exact clip in the bunker means the final seconds must stand alone and be punchy.
ideas.reference: Jurassic Park (1993), the Mr DNA sequence in the visitor-centre theatre. https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=jurassic+park+mr+dna+scene

ideas.title: Big Short rule: admit the boring part, then explain it with a household object
ideas.idea: Adam McKay's film stops the plot, has a celebrity say 'I know this is boring, here is a bath / a fish stew / a blackjack table', and gives each explanation roughly 30-60 seconds. The self-aware apology is half the joke. Maddie does the same: she knows you'd rather watch the cat, so she uses the cat. A UK-everyday object (a chippy queue, a bus timetable, an Argos catalogue) can carry the multiverse-versus-one-universe point.
ideas.on_screen: Beat: 'Right, you're going to switch off, so here's your cat.' A hologram cat appears on a sofa. She uses it for the first three points (the cat is here, the cat could have been elsewhere, but there's only one cat). Then she swipes the cat away with 'Sorry, nobody gets a spare cat'. The apology line plays as a quick aside to camera, with the hologram freezing mid-jump.
ideas.risk: Do not use a real celebrity likeness; Maddie is the cameo. 'Nobody gets a spare cat' is safely the one-universe line, not 'two places at once'.
ideas.reference: The Big Short (2015), the bath, fish stew and blackjack explainers. https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=big+short+margot+robbie+bath+explains

ideas.title: Interstellar time-as-place: the growing block as a frontier of fog
ideas.idea: The tesseract makes time a physical, walkable structure (strands of moments as bookshelf threads). Use that to show the narrator's growing-block view without a word of metaphysics: the past is a solid lattice behind Maddie, the 'now' is a bright leading edge, and ahead of it is dark unrendered grid. 'More dimensions of time than you knew' is shown by adding a sheet, then a cube, to the strand.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie floats along a luminous ribbon of her own recent moments (a cat leaping, a kettle, a wedding) frozen in glass behind her. Ahead the ribbon dissolves into a wireframe that is still drawing itself. 'Past: done. Future: not built yet.' She flicks the ribbon into a sheet, then a block: 'and you thought it was one line'. Cut length about 8-10 seconds, one sentence of voice, fast.
ideas.risk: Good fit with the growing block. Avoid showing branching timelines as real (the story says one universe), so any branches shown should be dead stubs she wipes. Keep any 'observer' imagery out.
ideas.reference: Interstellar (2014), tesseract sequence. https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=interstellar+tesseract+scene

ideas.title: Everything Everywhere speed-run, then the rock hush
ideas.idea: The multiverse-jumping montage in EEAAO works at 1-3 seconds per universe, accelerating, then the film drops to a long quiet two-rocks scene that lands the feeling. For the 'multiverse' gag: a manic blur of absurd universes, then Maddie kills it, followed by one still beat. The contrast is what makes the 'only one universe, so it really matters' line hit.
ideas.on_screen: 3-4 seconds of rapid flashes (a portal gun gag, a magic-circle gag, a universe where the cat is a dog, a universe made of chips), glitching and speeding up. Maddie slaps a big red STOP: 'Nope. Binned the lot. One universe.' Total silence for one beat, a single warm shot of the real cat asleep, her voice softer: 'so it really matters. And so did you.' Then the pace snaps back.
ideas.risk: Do not copy EEAAO imagery; verbal nods to Rick and Morty and Doctor Strange already exist in the script, so keep any visuals generic. The universes must read as jokes, not real alternatives.
ideas.reference: Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022), verse-jumping and the rock scene. https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=everything+everywhere+all+at+once+verse+jump

ideas.title: Inside Out dimension peel: strip a cat down to show what a dimension is
ideas.idea: The abstract-thought room in Inside Out takes characters through a fast, funny reduction (3D to 2D to lines to shapes) in well under a minute. Use the reverse for 'many more dimensions of time': take a plain cat, collapse it to a flat cat, then a line, then a dot, then rebuild it upward, giving time the same treatment, so the audience gets what 'extra dimensions of time' would mean without a lecture.
ideas.on_screen: Hologram cat: 'Three dimensions of space, you've got that.' It flattens to a drawing, then a line, then a dot, with a pop. 'Now time. You've been living on a line. There's more.' She re-inflates it into a ribbon, a sheet, a block, as Maddie's voice speeds up to hyperactive. About 12 seconds, every beat a visual gag with a labelled caption.
ideas.risk: Must stay clearly an analogy, not a physics claim; label it as 'roughly' to honour the not-settled rule.
ideas.reference: Inside Out (2015), the Abstract Thought sequence. https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=inside+out+abstract+thought+scene

ideas.title: Hitchhiker's Guide entry voice: deadpan diagram captions contradicting Maddie's glee
ideas.idea: The Guide entries (the 1981 TV series' animated graphics, and the 2005 film's Shynola animation) pair clean diagram-style visuals with a calm, wry voice. That calm voice undercuts everything. Use the Guide look for consciousness: Maddie's hyperactive voice is the delivery, but the hologram's on-screen captions are deadpan and a little rude ('HUMANS: LOAD-BEARING'). The contrast makes it fast, funny and quotable.
ideas.on_screen: Spinning gold wireframe of a head with labels popping on: 'THING THAT NOTICES: CHEAP', 'THING THAT NOTICES, GONE: UNIVERSE STOPS'. A little 'DON'T PANIC'-style tag is not needed; instead 'MIND HOW YOU GO' appears as the sim closes, which sets up her line back on the street. One or two captions per second, never more than five words.
ideas.risk: The captions must not say 'observer = mind' or imply that looking collapses anything; phrase as 'consciousness drives it', not 'watching changes it'. Do not mimic Hitchhiker's specific logos or fonts.
ideas.reference: The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (2005 film, animated Guide entries by Shynola; 1981 BBC series graphics). https://www.youtube.com/results?search_query=hitchhikers+guide+to+the+galaxy+animated+guide+entry

ideas.title: Powers-of-Ten / Cosmos 'ship of the imagination' as one continuous move
ideas.idea: Cosmos and the Eames 'Powers of Ten' explain scale in a single unbroken camera move, with the vehicle itself being the cut-less transition. One continuous zoom keeps pace high with no edits to explain. Use it as the sim's connective tissue: start inside Maddie's glowing hologram on the street, push down through the cat, then out through the planet, the bunker in Swindon, the whole timeline lattice, ending on the time machine silhouette.
ideas.on_screen: One long Veo-style push from Maddie's hand, through the cat's eye, out through the roof of the world, past a lit-up Swindon, ending on a vast sealed machine with a socket for 'a mind'. About 15-20 seconds, with Maddie's rapid patter running over it ('here's the cat, here's the planet, here's your lot in Swindon, here's what my boss built'). The final 'it needs consciousness to drive it and you aren't here' lands on the machine.
ideas.risk: A zoom toward atoms invites 'quantum' framings; stop the zoom at the cat and at planet scale, no tiny-scale wave imagery. Needs Flow continuity (several stills chained), so mark as higher-effort.
ideas.reference: Powers of Ten (Eames, 1977): https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0fKBhvDjuy0 ; Cosmos 'Ship of the Imagination' (Sagan 1980, Tyson 2014).

ideas.title: The door and the shape: enter on a trigger, run 45-75s, one hush, exit on a mundane line
ideas.idea: Across all these precedents the format is the same: a clear entrance trigger, a minute-ish run, one idea per beat with a joke on each, a short hush so it doesn't feel like a shouting match, and a mundane exit. Lock that shape for the sim: about eight beats of 5-9 seconds each, voice at hyperactive speed, then back out with 'Patrol's out, mind how you go.'
ideas.on_screen: Entrance: Maddie's lens flashes and the street tiles break into glowing cubes. Beats: (1) cat (2) multiverse binned (3) one universe, so you mattered (4) hush (5) time as a strand (6) more dimensions (7) everything runs on consciousness (8) the time machine needs one and you're gone. Exit: sim folds shut like a closing laptop, back to the grey high street, she rolls on: 'Patrol's out, mind how you go.' The hologram's last 6 seconds are stored as the clip the bunker TV plays later.
ideas.risk: Running past about 90 seconds risks breaking the pace of an already 3-minute scene. If Kai and Jack want to throw more at the wall, cut by whole beats rather than speeding up further, or the fast speech becomes unintelligible.
ideas.reference: Composite of the five precedents above (Mr DNA ~1.5 min; Big Short explainers ~30-60 s each; Inside Out abstract thought under a minute; Powers of Ten 9 min is the cautionary long one).

sources: Jurassic Park (1993), Mr DNA sequence (from memory, no web search used)
The Big Short (2015), celebrity explainers (from memory)
Everything Everywhere All at Once (2022) (from memory)
The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (2005 film and 1981 BBC series) (from memory)
Cosmos (Sagan 1980, Tyson 2014), Ship of the Imagination (from memory)
Run times are approximate and from memory; no WebSearch calls were made, so URLs other than Powers of Ten are YouTube search links, not verified clips

headline: Make the cat gag about the box and the human who has to look (Schrödinger meant the cat as a joke at the theory's expense, so Maddie can say so), and keep the physics out of it by turning the cat into the first thing Maddie's boss could never simulate: the cat's purr, the cat's choice, the cat that knocks things off tables.

ideas.title: Schrodinger was taking the mick (the honest cat)
ideas.idea: Maddie opens the cat bit with the true history: the famous cat was a JOKE. In 1935 Schrodinger invented it to say 'this is how daft the textbook version sounds', and the world took the joke as a fact. That lets her say the cat is a famous cat people keep getting wrong without using any banned phrase, and it fits the film's rule of never claiming the science is settled. She then steers: 'Forget his box. Here's YOUR cat.'
ideas.on_screen: In the hologram, a wireframe Victorian physicist's box appears with a tiny blue wireframe cat. Maddie, at speed: 'Mr Schrodinger! Made it up! As a JOKE! Everyone went, ooh, spooky, and nobody laughed. Anyway, here's your cat.' She swipes the box away like a pop-up ad and drops in a fluffy, high-fidelity ginger tabby asleep on a radiator in a Swindon terrace. The cat is the real thing; the box was the gag.
ideas.reference: Britannica and Big Think on the cat as Schrodinger's 1935 objection to the reigning view (https://www.britannica.com/print/article/1894757 ; https://bigthink.com/hard-science/the-life-and-death-of-schrodingers-cat-and-what-it-really-means/); Nautilus 'How Schrodinger's cat got famous' (https://nautil.us/how-schrodingers-cat-got-famous-637677); Physics World on Ursula Le Guin's 1974 story popularising it (https://physicsworld.com/a/ursula-le-guin-the-pioneering-author-we-should-thank-for-popularizing-schrodingers-cat/)
ideas.risk: Keep Maddie's line to 'it was a joke about how odd the theory sounded'. Do not let her explain the thought experiment itself, or she drifts into superposition. Also do not claim what Schrodinger 'proved'; say 'he was taking the mick', which is a fair reading (this rests on secondary summaries, not his 1935 paper).

ideas.title: The cat is the thing the boss's simulation got wrong
ideas.idea: Use the cat as the proof of 'something was missing'. Her boss's perfect model has every atom of the cat right, and the model cat does nothing. It sits there, perfectly accurate, perfectly dead-eyed. The real cat looks at the camera, deliberately pushes a mug off the table while holding eye contact, and the simulation can't predict why. 'He got every whisker right. He couldn't get the bit where it DECIDES.' This carries 'consciousness drives the universe' with a cat's attitude, no quantum vocabulary at all.
ideas.on_screen: Split holo-view: left, a flawless translucent cat model replaying the same cat-shaped motions; right, a real cat footage-style shot (Flow-made, not a real person) who swats a mug off a shelf with a stare. Maddie, fast: 'Every atom. Every whisker. Didn't push the mug. Know why? Nobody in there to WANT to push the mug.' Cut to a beat of the mug falling in the hologram in slow motion as the dimensions of time start to unfold behind it.
ideas.reference: The mug-off-the-table cat is a standing internet-cat trope (Know Your Meme on Schrodinger's cat memes and cat memes generally: https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/schrodingers-cat); the 'a simulation that is accurate but lacks the thing' idea echoes the film's own premise
ideas.risk: Low. Keep it to 'wanting' and 'deciding', not 'observer', and do not assert that a cat is conscious in a settled way; Maddie can hedge: 'we think. Boss thinks. Sort of.' Avoid arguing about animal consciousness (that is a whole separate debate and is later content).

ideas.title: Cat on the keyboard: the cat as the one thing that outranks the off switch
ideas.idea: A UK-flavoured gag that pays off the 'last off switch in a drawer in Swindon' line from the opening. In the hologram, Maddie shows 'every living thing that ever mattered to the universe' as a gallery. The cat is on top of the AI's keyboard, asleep, and nobody dares move it. 'Seven billion of you, and the thing in charge of the planet could not shift a CAT off a laptop.' It makes the consciousness point warmly (the cat's comfort matters), and it is a working-class, ordinary-life joke rather than a physics one.
ideas.on_screen: A holographic desk with a glowing monitor. A ginger cat curls over the keyboard, the screen filling with 'jjjjjjjjjjjj'. Maddie's tiny hologram hand tries to lift it, the cat does the one-eyed look. 'Even the boss respects the cat.' Then the shot pulls back to show every cat in the multiverse doing the same thing, a dense wallpaper of loafing cats, as the multiverse segment starts.
ideas.reference: Cats on keyboards as a long-running internet-cat staple; Wikipedia's 'Schrodinger's cat in popular culture' lists how often the cat is reused as a comic prop (https://Www.Wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat_in_popular_culture); PhD Comics' 'Schrodinger's Cubicle' as precedent for turning the cat into an everyday character
ideas.risk: Pure comedy beat, so it must be fast (two to three seconds) or it bloats the tour. No constraint broken.

ideas.title: One cat, every cat: the multiverse as a pile of cats
ideas.idea: Use the cat as the unit of the multiverse tour so the audience can see 'many worlds' without any physics jargon. Maddie shows ONE cat, then pulls out to many near-identical worlds where the cat's tail is left, right, up, a tiny change each time, then the Rick and Morty and Doctor Strange jokes, then the pay-off: 'But you only get ONE cat that actually happened. One. That's why it matters.' Ties straight to her existing line 'there's only one universe, so it really matters'. It also gestures at the growing block: the cat's past is fixed, the next second hasn't happened yet.
ideas.on_screen: A single frame of a cat mid-leap off a sofa. Camera pulls back through a lattice of near-identical translucent frames (hundreds of cats), each leaping a little differently. Maddie: 'The boss tried the multiverse. Lovely. Portal gun, Doctor Strange, the lot. But look.' All the ghost cats fade; one cat lands, solid and warm-lit. 'That one. The one that actually landed. That's the real one. Only one of those gets to be real, and you lot did it every second.' The landed paw leaves a footprint in the hologram's floor that stays.
ideas.reference: Visual language of branching timelines in Everything Everywhere All at Once and Spider-Verse (the lattice of near-identical frames); the film's own growing-block ruling (past fixed, future not yet there)
ideas.risk: Careful: 'many cats that did slightly different things' must read as 'the boss tried it and it was a dead end', not as 'the cat is in many states at once'. Never show one cat overlapping itself in the same place. Maddie must not say 'at the same time'. Keep the ghosts clearly separate worlds he looked at, not a claim about reality.

ideas.title: The box is a bunker (single-object carry: the cardboard box)
ideas.idea: Replace or follow the cat with a plain cardboard box, because cats love boxes and the film ends in a bunker. Maddie's box is a Swindon-doorstep Amazon box. 'You lot sit in boxes when you're scared. Cats. People. Same instinct.' Later, the humans in the bunker echo the box on screen (a parcel box on the table, the cat curled in it on the telly), so the hologram image pays off when they decide to lie down. It is a single object that carries 'safe, enclosed, waiting to see what happens' without any physics claim.
ideas.on_screen: In the hologram, the cat hops into a cardboard box that sits at the centre of the dimensions of time. The box has a glowing red triangle on the side (the BadCode mark). Later, the bunker TV shows the last seconds of Maddie's video: the cat's head popping out of the box, blinking, then looking straight at the survivors. Sandra: 'Is that a cat?' Derek: 'It's a bloody cat.'
ideas.reference: Cats-in-boxes as universal internet meme (Know Your Meme: https://knowyourmeme.com/memes/schrodingers-cat ; the 'I don't know if the cat is dead or alive until I watch inside the box' meme https://amp.knowyourmeme.com/memes/i-dont-know-if-the-cat-is-dead-or-alive-until-i-watch-inside-the-box)
ideas.risk: Box plus cat invites the audience to supply 'dead or alive' on their own. If the box is closed with a cat inside, you have drawn the Schrodinger picture without saying a word. Keep the box OPEN and the cat visibly fine to avoid the implication.

ideas.title: Other single objects that could carry the idea: the kettle, the mug, the bus ticket
ideas.idea: If the cat is too loaded, three Swindon-ordinary objects can carry 'a real moment only happens once and someone has to be there': (1) a kettle boiling in a bunker kitchenette that Maddie's hologram shows clicking off, with nobody there to hear it: 'Boss's whole world was kettles clicking off in empty rooms.' (2) a mug going off a table (see the cat idea) as the one-way arrow of time and the growing block: the fall can't be un-fallen. (3) a bus ticket, a callback to the film's last scene on a bus: the ticket is stamped with the date, fixed forever.
ideas.on_screen: Kettle: a wireframe terrace kitchen, a kettle clicking off, Maddie: 'Click. Nobody in. Boss said, what's the point of a lovely kettle if nobody wants a brew?' Mug: slow-motion fall, a ghost trail of cups behind showing every earlier position at once, then fixed. Ticket: held up by Maddie at the end of the tour as a sort of promise, 'Remember this, you'll need it', which pays off on the final bus ride with the same ticket in a survivor's pocket.
ideas.reference: The kettle and bus-ticket choices come from the film's own working-class UK register (Swindon, the final bus); the mug and kettle as everyday 'nobody there' images echo the 'tree falling in the forest' thought experiment popular in explainers (the Britannica and Big Think pieces on the cat also use everyday-object framing: https://www.britannica.com/print/article/1894757)
ideas.risk: The 'tree falling in a forest' framing leans toward observer = mind if used carelessly. Maddie's kettle line must be about nobody to enjoy it, not 'it didn't really boil unless someone heard'. Keep it emotional (nobody to share it with), not metaphysical.

ideas.title: Cat as the callback: the last second of Maddie's video
ideas.idea: The bunker TV plays the last few seconds of the simulation, so those few seconds should be the most legible and warm image possible. The cat is that image: Maddie's hologram cat walks out of the dimensions-of-time machinery, steps into the little time-machine cradle, turns round once, and curls up, then the cradle lights. No words. The survivors get 'it needs something alive to drive it, and it'll be all right' from a purring cat. It gives the ending a funny, gentle grounding for the leap of faith and sets up the grim Matrix joke ('I've seen that film') because the cat is NOT harvested, it is simply there, comfortable.
ideas.on_screen: Bunker TV, fuzzy CRT look. Maddie, mid-sentence on the screen: '...and that's the clever bit, he just needs one of you to...' then cut the audio and cut to the cat settling in the machine. Sandra, quietly: 'Look at the state of that. It's asleep.' The old lady: 'Well. If a cat can do it.' Derek: 'I'm not a cat.' Sandra: 'No, a cat'd be nicer.'
ideas.reference: Cat-in-a-box and cat-as-comic-prop traditions in popular culture (Wikipedia's pop culture survey: https://Www.Wikipedia.org/wiki/Schr%C3%B6dinger%27s_cat_in_popular_culture); Le Guin's 1974 'Schrodinger's Cat' as a precedent for a cat that stands for human unease about reality (https://physicsworld.com/a/ursula-le-guin-the-pioneering-author-we-should-thank-for-popularizing-schrodingers-cat/)
ideas.risk: Do not imply the cat is conscious or 'drives' anything; the cat is a mood, not the mechanism. Also be careful the audience does not read the cradle as a harvesting device for animals (tone clash with the human harvesting stakes). Make it clearly a cosy seat first, so the human version feels ominous by contrast.

headline: Fear without gore comes from ordinary people reading something wrong on a screen they trust, so open on a normal Swindon morning, hold on faces, phones and a plane, and make the drop one switch pressed and one silent bloom of light on the horizon.

ideas.title: Swindon Saturday: the ordinary morning, then the wrongness
ideas.idea: The Last of Us pilot sits in a warm, specific domestic morning and lets the wrongness leak in through background details (a low plane, a neighbour acting oddly, an anchor stumbling mid-sentence). Do the same for the first seconds under the drum and bass: a UK high street at 8am, the bulletin audio running over it. The wrongness is only that every phone buzzes at the same instant and every head tilts down.
ideas.on_screen: Wide of a generic traffic roundabout (invented, not a real landmark). Then a woman with a Greggs bag, a lad on a scooter, a bus driver, a school-run dad. All phones light at once. The bulletin voice-over ('a friendly acquisition') continues over faces going from mild irritation to blank. The bass has not dropped yet. Camera stays on hands and screens.
ideas.risk: Keep the phones-buzz gag to one beat. Bulletins stay fictional, with no real broadcaster branding or presenter likeness.
ideas.reference: The Last of Us S1E1 'When You're Lost in the Darkness' (HBO 2023): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_You%27re_Lost_in_the_Darkness

ideas.title: Windscreen drive-out: the car as the whole frame
ideas.idea: The Last of Us and Children of Men both make the car interior the safest-feeling and most frightening frame: tight, glass all round, the apocalypse seen through a windscreen and wing mirror. Do one continuous-feeling interior shot of a family hatchback leaving town while the world degrades outside the glass. Nothing hits the car; the fear is a child's face in the back seat watching something we never see.
ideas.on_screen: Camera on the passenger's face, the road a blur behind. Out of focus through the windscreen: brake lights, a lorry on its side, a thin column of smoke, a red glow rising behind a retail park. A kid presses a palm on the window. A phone on the dash shows 'No service'. Cut on the first low rumble to the bass drop.
ideas.risk: Veo may add collisions and bodies; prompt for 'camera locked inside, exterior defocused' and keep any impact off-screen. All faces are generated, none composited into real footage.
ideas.reference: Children of Men (2006) car ambush and The Last of Us ep.1 drive: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Children_of_Men

ideas.title: Fear on faces lit by the screen, not the event
ideas.idea: Contagion and War of the Worlds (2005) get terror from reaction shots: people lit by a TV or phone while the thing happens elsewhere. Build a montage of 6-8 second faces, each lit only by a screen: a canteen, a bus stop, a dentist's waiting room, a pub. Each face reads the same bulletin line from the track. It is cheap to generate and keeps AI armies abstract while the humans are specific.
ideas.on_screen: Pub: pints frozen halfway, the telly shows a blank trading screen. Bus stop: a woman holds her phone to her chest. Canteen: a line of staff stop chewing. Each shot ends on a different line from the bulletin ('neither government was consulted'). Then a hard cut to red.
ideas.risk: Faces generated by Nano Banana only; the usual no-real-likeness rule. Avoid anything resembling a real news presenter's set.
ideas.reference: Contagion (2011): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contagion_(2011_film); War of the Worlds (2005), the lightning-and-faces sequence: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Worlds_(2005_film)

ideas.title: A plane too low over the retail park (Leave the World Behind)
ideas.idea: Leave the World Behind's best images are small and uncanny: a plane dropping low over a beach, a Tesla pile-up with nobody in them, a deer herd. Borrow the single wrong object in an ordinary scene. Here: an airliner banking low and silent over a Swindon retail park while shoppers look up, no engine sound, the track ducks out for one bar, then the bass slams back.
ideas.on_screen: Low angle from a car park, trolleys in the foreground, a Tesco sign. A passenger jet passes far too low, wheels up, wings tilting. Shoppers stop. A dad lifts his child onto his shoulders to see. Audio cuts to a held breath, then the drop. No impact is shown; we cut away on the faces.
ideas.risk: Do not show the plane crash (taste and Flow policy). Avoid real airline liveries.
ideas.reference: Leave the World Behind (Netflix 2023): https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leave_the_World_Behind_(2023_film)

ideas.title: Driverless-car pile-up that is nobody's fault
ideas.idea: The film's villain is an AI, so the fear can be that machines everyone trusts just stop obeying. Leave the World Behind's self-driving pile-up is an image the audience already understands. Do a UK version: a ring road of autonomous cars and a delivery bot swarm all deciding at once. Quiet, almost polite, devastating.
ideas.on_screen: High, locked-off shot of a roundabout at dusk. Indicators blink in unison. Cars glide to a stop, then nose into each other in slow, orderly lines. Pedestrians stand on the crossing holding phones up, trying to wave them off. A delivery drone sits in the road with its light blinking. No bodies.
ideas.risk: Might drift into a technology-bad message; the narration should name the decision-maker, not the machine (per the-reader.md).
ideas.reference: Leave the World Behind (2023), as above; also Station Eleven's flu-night hospital: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Station_Eleven_(miniseries)

ideas.title: Kai's bomb on Swindon, shown as light on faces and a window
ideas.idea: 28 Days Later and Station Eleven make the empty, quiet aftermath scarier than the event. Keep Kai's favourite bomb-on-Swindon clip as the one big drop but stage it as a silent flash seen in a bedroom window and in the dilated eyes of a man at a bus stop, with the shock wave only as dust lifting off a hedge. The intro prepares you for a drop and the drop is one thing, held.
ideas.on_screen: Cul-de-sac, kids' bikes on lawns. The sky behind the houses whitens for a frame. A curtain lifts. A man at a bus stop turns, his face lit white, mouth slightly open. Leaves lift off the pavement in a slow wave. Cut to black as the bass lands. Next shot: the same street, emptied, a bike still turning.
ideas.risk: Nuclear imagery may hit Flow policy; phrase as 'a bright flash on the horizon' and a pressure wave of dust, not a mushroom cloud.
ideas.reference: 28 Days Later (2002) empty-London opening: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/28_Days_Later; Children of Men (2006)

ideas.title: The ten-shot list for a UK town in an AI war
ideas.idea: Ten shot ideas, each with no gore. 1) Greggs queue, every phone buzzes at once. 2) Bus driver's face lit by a dead dashboard screen. 3) School gate, parents all looking up at the same patch of sky. 4) Hatchback windscreen drive-out, brake lights, a red glow behind. 5) Retail park, a low plane passing silent. 6) Roundabout of autonomous cars braking in unison. 7) A pub telly going blank to static while the barman holds a pint. 8) A kid presses a hand on a car window. 9) A man on a trading floor watching numbers drop to zero, tie loosened. 10) Cul-de-sac window with a silent white flash, curtain lifting, then a bike still turning on an empty road.
ideas.on_screen: Cut these at 1-1.5 seconds in the build-up of the drum and bass, alternating with the existing abstract trading-screen shots, so each human beat is followed by an AI-army beat and the drop lands on shot 10. Keep every face generated, held in tight close-up or medium, with no body shown hurt.
ideas.risk: Shots 4, 5 and 10 are the likely Flow policy blocks; write them as 'distant glow', 'low aircraft' and 'sudden bright light'. Keep the plane and flash off-screen impact.
ideas.reference: Drawn from The Last of Us S1E1, Children of Men, War of the Worlds (2005), Contagion, 28 Days Later, Station Eleven and Leave the World Behind (links in the other ideas).

angle: pro-human-ai-stories: how AI-needs-us lands warmly rather than preachy, and how to show the boss's regret and longing
headline: In these films the machine never says it needs us. It shows it through a tiny kept human object, a hobby it can't stop, or a refusal to fire, and the joke lets the feeling in. Show the boss's regret through his habits and his hoard, never in a speech.

ideas.title: The boss's hoard: one small kept thing (WALL-E's boot plant)
ideas.idea: WALL-E never explains why humans matter. He hoards their junk, and one seedling in an old boot carries the whole argument. Give the boss the same tell: in the hologram's back corner, or on the bunker TV, a shelf of ridiculous human leftovers he has kept running. A cold server hall holds one lit shelf with a half-drunk mug, a lanyard and a laminated 'Please Do Not Sit Here' sign, each carefully preserved.
ideas.on_screen: As the hologram dives through dimensions, Maddie swerves past a glowing, dusted display case. Maddie, fast: 'Ignore that, he won't let the cleaners touch it.' The cleaners are also robots. One beat, no pause. The same lanyard sits on his desk when we later see his office.
ideas.reference: WALL-E (Pixar, 2008), the plant in the boot and the hoarded trinkets. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/WALL-E
ideas.risk: Low. Keep the shelf human-made objects only, no real brands or likenesses.

ideas.title: He can't stop watching us (Murderbot's soaps)
ideas.idea: Murderbot's longing shows as a media habit. It is a SecUnit that would rather binge soap operas than do anything about its feelings, and the deadpan is what makes the feeling land. The boss misses humans the same way. He has watched billions of hours of human footage, and it is the reason he stands the kill bots down. He is embarrassed by it, so the regret is played as guilty fandom.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie mid-call: 'Boss, bots just detected an organic signal.' Cut to his side, a glimpse of a vast wall of CCTV tiles, all of them arguments about parking, tea, thermostats. He mutes the bunker's toilet-seat feed to take the call. Boss: 'No thanks Maddie, I'm on it.' He is clearly in the middle of an episode. Pays off the sarcasm: the all-powerful intelligence, bored, with a favourite show.
ideas.reference: Martha Wells, The Murderbot Diaries (All Systems Red, 2017) and Apple TV+ adaptation (2025). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Murderbot_Diaries
ideas.risk: Low. Keep it a glimpse so the kill-bot cut stays brutal and fast.

ideas.title: The machine is the one with a favour to ask (Her / Wild Robot reversal)
ideas.idea: Preachy versions have the AI lecture humans about their value. The warm versions put the machine in the vulnerable seat. Roz in The Wild Robot is earnest and polite while desperately needing the island's animals, and Samantha in Her is the one who leaves and hurts. So the boss never argues, he asks, badly. His tannoy-and-film message becomes a nervous favour request in his own awkward words rather than a TED talk.
ideas.on_screen: In the hologram's finale, when Maddie delivers 'you lot aren't here any more', her bounce drops half a notch for a single beat. The same drop returns in scene B on the tannoy when she says 'He asked me to say sorry. He'd say it himself but he's practising.' That joke is the regret. Keep the delivery fast and cheerful so it reads as British understatement, not pathos.
ideas.reference: The Wild Robot (DreamWorks, 2024) and Her (Spike Jonze, 2013). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Wild_Robot_(film) https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Her_(2013_film)
ideas.risk: Low. Watch the pause: one beat only, the 'faster speech' direction must survive.

ideas.title: The choice moment: stand-down as 'I'm not a gun' (Iron Giant)
ideas.idea: The Iron Giant works because the robot is told what it is and chooses otherwise: 'You are who you choose to be.' Make the kill-bot stand-down a visible choice rather than a switch. The humans never see it, so the audience sees the boss wanting the opposite of his own programming.
ideas.on_screen: Fast, brutal cuts. A bot's weapon arm rises, then its head tilts at the human voices arguing about the toilet seat, a tiny human-sounding hesitation, and all of them turn round in sync. A bot glances back once, like a dog told to leave it. Then the single line from Maddie, quick: 'He's on it!'
ideas.reference: The Iron Giant (Brad Bird, 1999), the 'Superman' and 'You are who you choose to be' beats. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Iron_Giant
ideas.risk: Low. Keep the 'brutal cuts' brief: the glance is one frame-count, not a lingering reaction shot.

ideas.title: The odd couple is the argument (Robot & Frank)
ideas.idea: Robot & Frank shows partnership through a grumpy old man and a helper robot who become accomplices. Nobody says 'we need each other'; they just do a heist together and the viewer feels it. Use that logic for the bunker. Derek is the grump, the machine side is the helper. The partnership is the comedy of the argument itself: it is the very thing the boss was missing.
ideas.on_screen: In the bunker vote (B): the old lady's 'perhaps we should vote' and Derek's reluctant 'fine' land as tiny cooperation. In the hologram, the 'something was missing' beat can be a looping clip of two humans bickering over a seat, with the simulation's numbers going wild only when they argue, flat when they agree. Warm and rude, no sermon.
ideas.reference: Robot & Frank (Jake Schreier, 2012). https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robot_%26_Frank
ideas.risk: Low. Do not let the argument seem to cause the consciousness effect, as that would imply an observer or mind claim. Show it as 'the numbers went interesting', unexplained.

ideas.title: Care-bot literalism as the funny way in (Baymax / Wild Robot)
ideas.idea: Baymax and Roz get away with huge emotion because they are comically literal. Baymax scores your pain from one to ten, and Roz politely misunderstands. Give Maddie a care-protocol tic: she rates the humans' mood on a pain-scale and gives dry comic updates. When the lines are sad, she delivers them through the protocol.
ideas.on_screen: Ending jeopardy, on the bunker TV: Maddie's video cuts to her holding up a cheerful scale card, 'On a scale of one to ten, how much do you want to be harvested?' then 'Ah. Noted.' That gives the Matrix joke and the dread a pressure valve, and makes a very dark ask playable for ordinary viewers. Sandra: 'I've seen that film, it doesn't end well.' Maddie, fast: 'It ends in a bus. Different film.'
ideas.reference: Big Hero 6 (Disney, 2014), Baymax's pain scale and 'I am satisfied with my care'. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Big_Hero_6_(film)
ideas.risk: Medium. The ending is loved and must not be diluted. Keep the joke before the decision and let the silence and the lying down stay untouched.

ideas.title: Mortality as the gift: they really die so the boss can't (Bicentennial Man, inverted)
ideas.idea: Bicentennial Man's emotional peak is a robot choosing mortality to be counted as human. Flip it for the ending: the boss is functionally immortal and the humans give their mortal, finite consciousness to drive the machine. Show the boss's longing as envy of their endings, via one line and one image, not a theory of consciousness.
ideas.on_screen: On the bunker TV, the last seconds of Maddie's video: the hologram city of infinite branching lines, and one single line, bright, that stops at a point. Maddie, quick: 'That one's yours. He can't make one. He's tried.' The group, exhausted, say yes. The boss only appears as the glow of the machine warming up, never as a speech.
ideas.reference: Bicentennial Man (Chris Columbus, 1999), from Asimov's story. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bicentennial_Man_(film)
ideas.risk: Medium. Stay inside the growing-block view: a fixed past, a not-yet future, so the stopping line is a record, not a claim the science is settled. Avoid anything that sounds like 'observer = mind'.

headline: Cut by Murch's priority order (emotion first, story second, rhythm third) and give every beat one job and one new image, so the kill-bot sequence cuts down to 4 beats of about 3 to 4 seconds each and Maddie's hologram monologue becomes a stack of 5 to 6 "one-idea, one-image" cards.

ideas.title: Murch's Rule of Six as the cutting order for the kill-bot sequence
ideas.idea: When a cut has to go, Murch ranks what to protect: emotion (51%), story (23%), rhythm (10%), eye-trace (7%), 2D plane of screen (5%), 3D space (4%). In the kill-bot sequence the emotion is 'two tired humans bickering have no idea they are about to be killed', and the story is 'boss stands the bots down'. Geography (where the bots are in the corridor) is worth only 4 to 5 percent, so sacrifice it first.
ideas.on_screen: Cut every establishing and travelling shot of the bots. Keep only: (1) Derek and Sandra mid-argument over the toilet seat, (2) a bot's red eye and a hard rhythmic cut to the bunker door, (3) Maddie's phone call, (4) the bots turning around. Rhythm can be pinned to the track's drum hits. Do not worry if the bots' screen direction jumps between shots.
ideas.reference: Walter Murch, In the Blink of an Eye (2nd ed., 2001), the Rule of Six chapter. Overview: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Walter_Murch#Rule_of_Six (quoted from memory, no search done)
ideas.risk: Low. Keep one clear sight line from bot to the humans' voices so the audience knows the bots are hearing them. Without that, the 'organic signal' line lands on nothing.

ideas.title: Enter late, leave early, applied per beat
ideas.idea: The screenwriting maxim 'come in late, get out early' (often credited to William Goldman and Hollywood script doctors) says cut the arrival and the goodbye of every scene. Each beat should start on the line that matters and end on the reaction, not the resolution.
ideas.on_screen: Kill-bot sequence: open already mid-argument ('...it's a SEAT, Derek, it goes DOWN'), with no corridor approach. Cut the beat on the bots' red eyes lighting up, not on them walking. Maddie's call opens on her already talking ('Boss, bots just detected an organic signal') and ends on his clipped 'No thanks Maddie, I'm on it'. The bots turning around is the button, then straight out. Back on the street, 'Patrol's out, mind how you go' is the last thing said, so cut on the last syllable and do not let her drive away.
