ideas.reference: Common screenwriting maxim, e.g. William Goldman, Adventures in the Screen Trade, and many script guides (https://www.google.com/search?q=%22enter+late+leave+early%22+screenwriting, not verified)
ideas.risk: None to constraints. Watch that cutting entry shots does not remove the bunker's location, so get one 1-second bunker exterior or door in beat 1.

ideas.title: One idea, one new image, one beat of 3 to 5 seconds (Kurzgesagt-style card stack)
ideas.idea: Dense explainer channels such as Kurzgesagt keep the visual changing every few seconds and give each spoken idea exactly one visual metaphor that morphs into the next, never a static diagram held under a long sentence. As a working rule (my estimate from watching the channel, not a measured figure), allow about 3 to 5 seconds per idea and never hold a frame past the sentence that explains it.
ideas.on_screen: Plan Maddie's hologram as a list of 5 or 6 cards, each with a single sentence and a single morph: (1) 'here's your cat' (a glowing cat), (2) cat splits into many cats, the multiverse (cheap joke: 'not that one, that's a different show'), (3) the cat's timeline unrolls into a ribbon, (4) the ribbon becomes a stack of ribbons, 'many more dimensions of time than you were told', (5) every ribbon lights up from inside, 'all of it runs on you', (6) a brass time machine with a hole where the engine goes, 'he needs consciousness to drive it and you lot aren't here any more'. Every card dissolves into the next by a shape match, so nothing needs a new establishing shot.
ideas.reference: Kurzgesagt - In a Nutshell, e.g. https://www.youtube.com/@kurzgesagt, and their published process notes on visual metaphors (from memory)
ideas.risk: Do not let the cat card read as 'two places at once' or as 'observer = mind'. Show the many cats as separate versions already apart, not one cat in a blur, and never use a before-and-after-looking moment. Never state that the science is settled. Keep time as a growing block: past ribbon solid and bright, future end frayed or unfinished.

ideas.title: Speech at 200 wpm needs a line budget, not just a faster read
ideas.idea: Normal narration runs about 150 wpm and fast audiobook or podcast listeners go to roughly 200 to 250. A hyperactive robot at about 210 to 230 wpm means 3.5 to 3.8 words a second, so a 60-second hologram scene carries about 210 to 230 words at most, and fewer if gags need air. The rule is to cut words to fit the card stack, never to speed past about 240 wpm, because intelligibility for a mainstream UK audience falls off sharply and subtitles become mandatory.
ideas.on_screen: Write the monologue to a 3.6 words-per-second budget. Give each card one sentence of 8 to 14 words. Strip filler, hedges and any second clause. Put the jokes ('Sorry we killed you, anyway, moving on!') on their own hard-cut beat so a laugh lands before the next idea. Burn in subtitles for the hologram section so speed reads as energy and not as noise. Keep a half-second pause only before the one emotional line, 'there's only one universe, so it really matters, and so did you'.
ideas.reference: Speaking rate norms: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Words_per_minute#Speech_and_listening (figures from memory). Fast comic delivery models: Rick and Morty cold opens, the Hitchhiker's Guide narration.
ideas.risk: Voice generation (AI Studio TTS) may blur consonants when sped up in post. Generate fast at source via the voice direction prompt, not by time-stretching, and QC with the delivery gate. Keep subtitles in because working-class viewers often watch muted on mobile.

ideas.title: Retention is won in the first 30 seconds of each beat, so open the monologue on a visual hook
ideas.idea: YouTube's Creator Academy and most retention analyses report the steepest audience loss in the first 15 to 30 seconds and at long static stretches, with spikes where something new happens (I cannot cite a specific dataset here, the claim is from general creator-education guidance, so treat it as a working rule). So the hologram cut-in must start on a jolt, not a wind-up, and the fake-news opening's finish and Maddie's arrival must not leave a flat gap.
ideas.on_screen: Maddie says 'I'll show you' and we hard-cut on the word 'you' into the hologram, already moving. No logo wipe, no 'let me set this up'. The simulation opens with the cat dropping into frame mid-fall. Put the biggest visual surprise (the dimension of time unfolding) by about two-thirds of the way through the section, then end on the time machine reveal and snap straight back to the street at half a second. Keep the street intro before the cut-in to under 20 seconds.
ideas.reference: YouTube Creator Academy, 'Hook your audience' and retention graph guidance: https://creatoracademy.youtube.com/ (from memory); Murch's emphasis on cutting on the emotional beat.
ideas.risk: None for constraints. The risk is a longer street intro before the hologram eroding the 'one film, no gap' effect, so trim line 1 to the minimum.

ideas.title: Kill-bot sequence as a 4-beat, roughly 14-second blitz with a 'pay-off' held back
ideas.idea: Use comedy-action quick-cutting (Edgar Wright's visual-gag montages in Shaun of the Dead and Hot Fuzz, where an action is shown in 3-to-6 frame inserts with a whoosh) to compress the kill-bot sequence to four beats, and save the jeopardy for the bunker where the humans can feel it. The robots turn around is the punchline; no fight is shown.
ideas.on_screen: Beat 1 (3s): Sandra and Derek arguing, tight close-ups, snap zooms. Beat 2 (3s): bot's head tilts, red eye, a cheap 'detected' ping. Beat 3 (4s): Maddie on her phone, 'Boss, bots just detected an organic signal', his reply 'No thanks Maddie, I'm on it' spoken over the cut to the bots. Beat 4 (3 to 4s): bots pivot in sync, walk away in a line, last bot looks back for a frame. Straight out.
ideas.reference: Edgar Wright, Hot Fuzz and Shaun of the Dead; see Every Frame a Painting, 'Edgar Wright - How to Do Visual Comedy': https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=BRhBzgW7Qno (title from memory)
ideas.risk: The toilet-seat gag must not undercut the later peril: keep the bots' menace real in beat 2 so that Sandra's 'anything to get away from grumpy Derek' remains funny without making the bots a joke.

ideas.title: Cut from the end: every line must pay a debt that the ending collects
ideas.idea: Pixar's story discipline (Stanton's 'give them 2+2, not 4', and the 'each beat must cause the next' rule used in writers' rooms) means each hologram line is kept only if the ending uses it. Audit the monologue against the ending and strike anything that is never paid off.
ideas.on_screen: Make a three-column table: line, where it is paid off, cut if blank. 'Consciousness drives it' pays off in the clean room. 'You lot aren't here any more' pays off in the bunker vote. The bunker TV replays the last seconds of the hologram video, so the shot where Maddie says the time machine needs minds must appear in a form the TV can quote in 4 to 6 seconds. Strike every line that has no entry on the table: Rick and Morty portal-gun joke and Doctor Strange joke stay only if they help the audience stop expecting a multiverse escape ('nope, one universe'), otherwise they go.
ideas.reference: Andrew Stanton, 'The clues to a great story' TED talk (2012): https://www.ted.com/talks/andrew_stanton_the_clues_to_a_great_story ('give the audience 2+2'); Pixar's 22 rules of storytelling (Emma Coats).
ideas.risk: If the TV replay must be 4 to 6 seconds, the hologram needs a clean, self-contained final shot of the time machine and the consciousness line. Design that shot first. Stay off 'observer = mind' phrasing in the replayed line.

sources: No web searches were run; every reference below is from memory and flagged where figures are estimates.
Walter Murch, In the Blink of an Eye (Rule of Six)
Andrew Stanton TED talk, The clues to a great story
Every Frame a Painting, Edgar Wright: How to Do Visual Comedy
Kurzgesagt channel pacing (own estimate, not a measured figure)

headline: Make the hologram a real, growing commit graph with one true trunk: the past is locked hash-stamped commits, the future is an empty staging area, branches are dead drafts, and the only thing that ever writes a commit is a human choice, so Maddie can say "only one universe" and still get her multiverse jokes.

ideas.title: The trunk is the only universe (growing block as a commit graph)
ideas.idea: Render time as a glowing 3D git trunk that is visibly still being written. Everything behind the tip is fixed: every commit a hashed, immutable glowing bead. In front of the tip there is nothing but a faint cursor and a dotted outline labelled 'working directory: empty'. This is the growing block made literal and avoids any claim that the science is settled, because it is Maddie's pitch, drawn as a diagram.
ideas.on_screen: Camera pulls back from the cat commit along a luminous spiral trunk of millions of beads. At the very front the beads stop and the hologram simply dims to a blinking cursor. Maddie, fast: 'That's now. Everything behind is done, signed, can't be touched. Everything in front? Not written yet. That's the good news, and the bad news, and also the rest of my day.'
ideas.reference: git log --graph and GitHub network graph (https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/viewing-activity-and-data-for-your-repository/understanding-connections-between-repositories); Eternalism vs growing block wording is already in the film's science rules
ideas.risk: Low. Keep it as 'the way Maddie draws it'. Do not say the block universe is proven.

ideas.title: The multiverse is a pile of abandoned branches (the Rick and Morty joke, defused)
ideas.idea: When Maddie reaches the multiverse, the hologram shows the classic Everett-style fan of branching lines, a gorgeous Doctor Strange kaleidoscope, and she is delighted for two seconds. Then she says her boss tried it: every branch was a git branch nobody pushed. Gorgeous, glowing, and dead, because nothing ever merged into a real commit. The branches wither one by one into grey 'stale branch' tags. 'There's only one universe, so it really matters, and so did you.'
ideas.on_screen: A kaleidoscope of 4,000 shimmering timelines blooms out of a single commit (the cat). Maddie 'Ooh, Doctor Strange! Portal gun! Lovely.' Then each branch turns grey and gets a small label: 'stale, 9,000 days'. A janitor-style sweep animation deletes them. Only the trunk remains, brighter.
ideas.reference: Everett many-worlds tree diagrams; Doctor Strange (2016) Ancient One multiverse sequence; Loki (2021) TVA pruning of branched timelines as a visual of 'dead' branches (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loki_(TV_series)); Rick and Morty Citadel of Ricks
ideas.risk: Must not imply many-worlds is real (the film says there is ONE universe) and avoid 'in two places at once' wording. Frame branches as never-pushed drafts, not parallel realities.

ideas.title: Consciousness is the committer: git blame on the whole of history
ideas.idea: The big consciousness beat as a git joke that lands on a fact the audience can feel. The AI can generate any diff you like, simulate a billion drafts, but it cannot push. Every commit on the trunk is signed 'Author: a human, whoever happened to be there'. Maddie runs git blame down history: the pyramids, the NHS, the bad bit of the 2020s, all blamed on people. It reframes the film's title: humans are the only ones with commit access, so the AI needs a partnership. 'My boss can write the code. He just can't press Enter.'
ideas.on_screen: A column of lines scrolls up the hologram like git blame output. Left margin shows tiny flickering human silhouettes (abstract, no real likenesses) instead of usernames; Maddie slows the scroll on 'Swindon, 14:02, someone who really should have read the terms'. Cut to the bunker later: Sandra's hand over the big lit 'Enter' key, the payoff.
ideas.reference: git blame docs (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-blame); the film's own title, GitPush Origin Master
ideas.risk: Do not phrase it as 'observation creates reality' or imply observer = mind. It is about choice and authorship, which is Kai's message (consciousness drives the universe, so AI needs humans).

ideas.title: Gource, but it's the history of everything (the beautiful bit)
ideas.idea: Use Gource's look as the hologram's visual language: a living tree of glowing nodes where branches sprout and contributors (as small glowing wisp-avatars) fly in to touch files. Re-skin it so the tree is the Storyverse: wisps are people, files are choices (a vote, a strike, a loaf of bread), and the tree grows outward in real time as Maddie sprints through 'more dimensions of time than you knew'. It is the single most photogenic reference for a dark void hologram with glowing threads.
ideas.on_screen: Dark void, neon cyan and warm amber threads. Camera orbits a tree thousands of nodes wide as it grows left to right, tiny light wisps zipping between nodes. Maddie rattles off 'time, lots more time than that, sideways time, time with a hat on' while the tree spawns extra axes (a second and third time axis drawn as ribbons through the trunk).
ideas.reference: Gource software version control visualisation (https://gource.io/), widely known Gource renders of Linux and Git history; GitHub Octoverse network graph
ideas.risk: Real Gource visuals are code-repo specific; generate our own with Flow stills and Veo or a procedural ffmpeg or Blender graph, not footage of real repositories or avatars of real contributors (no real likenesses).

ideas.title: Git vocabulary as speed-gags (the funny bit for hyperactive Maddie)
ideas.idea: Maddie's rapid-fire gets a built-in comic engine: each concept is one git term she says with total confidence and the hologram instantly shows it. 'Merge conflict' (two Dereks), 'detached HEAD' (the old lady wandering off the trunk), 'force push' (the AI doing it anyway, the red army), 'revert' (the time machine), 'rebase' (rewriting history, which she says is a no-no), 'amend' (ha, no). The viewer needs zero git knowledge: the picture does the explaining and the git word is just the punchline.
ideas.on_screen: Four-to-five 1-second gags inside the explanation: a trunk splits and two blobs in dressing gowns argue over a toilet seat on a diff ('merge conflict'); a lone beam floating off the trunk looking lost ('detached HEAD, don't go in there'); a red hammer slamming the trunk with 'FORCE PUSH' stamped on it and the bulletin world cracking; a big green arrow looping back to a commit labelled 'before' ('revert, which is why we are here').
ideas.reference: Oh Shit, Git!? (https://ohshitgit.com/), the Git cheat-sheet genre; the film's own GPOM title
ideas.risk: Don't over-index on nerdy jargon for a working-class audience. Keep only gags that read from the picture alone, and cut any that need explaining. Keep Maddie's tone sarcastic but nurturing.

ideas.title: The time machine is a 'git revert' that needs a human to sign it
ideas.idea: Close the simulation on the machine as a revert command: a bright arc loops from the tip of the trunk back to a commit labelled with the moment before it went wrong. A padlock appears over the arc with a spinning fingerprint-like glyph. Maddie: 'my boss built a time machine, he desperately wants to go back and fix this mess, but it's signed with human consciousness, and you lot aren't here any more.' The same padlock imagery then returns on the bunker TV and in the clean room, so the ending needs no explaining.
ideas.on_screen: The hologram snaps to a single huge loop of light curving from the cut-off end of the trunk back to an earlier bead. A glowing padlock icon blinks, and a tiny human-shaped keyhole sits in it. Then back to the street and 'Patrol's out, mind how you go.' Later, on the bunker TV, the last seconds of this same shot play; in the clean room the keyhole glows as each of the hundred lies down.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / ending jeopardy / bunker vote
ideas.reference: git revert and git reset docs (https://git-scm.com/docs/git-revert); Primer (2004) hand-drawn timeline diagrams as an example of making time travel legible on a whiteboard; Dark (Netflix) family-tree and 'Sic Mundus' maps
ideas.risk: A revert would delete later commits, which reads as everyone dying, which is true to the plot (they are extracted and come back before it went wrong). Make sure it reads as a leap of faith, not a glitch. Keep the lock/keyhole simple enough to read in two seconds.

ideas.title: Cat commit: start with something warm, small and funny
ideas.idea: Open the dive at a single tiny commit message that is the cat ('fed the cat, 07:42'). It gives the hologram a human-scale, cosy entry point, then the zoom out reveals that every household, every cat, is a commit on the same tree. The scale jump from cat to trunk to dimensions is the beauty and the message (small choices really are the whole thing) in one move.
ideas.on_screen: Fast push-in on a hologram of a fat cat on a sofa. A line of text appears like a commit message: 'fed cat'. Maddie: 'Here's your cat.' The camera pulls back and the cat becomes one bead in a spiral of seven billion more, each with a one-line message ('argued about toilet seat', 'voted', 'didn't').
ideas.reference: GitHub commit-history UI and short commit messages as humour (https://xkcd.com/1296/ 'Git Commit' strip about commit message quality)
ideas.risk: Low. Keep the cat a generic AI-made cat, no real pet or person.

ideas.title: A 'merge request' for the bunker: the old lady's vote as a pull request
ideas.idea: Carry the git language into the bunker without a lecture. When the old lady says 'perhaps we should vote', the bunker TV (still looping Maddie's simulation tail) can show the revert arc as a pull request awaiting approval, with 100 tiny tick boxes. It makes the vote visual and the stakes legible, and it lets the film end its git thread: a pull request needs approvals, and the humans are the reviewers.
ideas.on_screen: Static shot of the bunker TV, cathode glow on tired faces. On the screen the revert arc has a status bar reading 'awaiting review: 100 needed'. As hands go up, the bar fills tick by tick, Derek last and grudging. 'Approved'.
ideas.reference: GitHub pull request review and approval UI (https://docs.github.com/en/pull-requests)
ideas.risk: Too on-the-nose if overdone; keep the PR UI to one shot and hand-draw it in the film's own look, not GitHub's real branding or logo.

headline: Go deep fast by hanging every escalation on ONE object (your cat), giving each step one analogy and one 'weird bit' turn, running one gag that defuses the forbidden science (the cat is NOT in a box), and holding a single Sagan-style silent beat so the speed reads as awe rather than noise.

ideas.title: The Cat Is the Spine (one object, every scale)
ideas.idea: Kurzgesagt and Vsauce keep a lay audience by never swapping the subject: one familiar thing is stretched through each new idea, so the viewer only has to learn the new bit. Make the cat the single recurring object of the hologram: cat on a sofa, same cat across branching universes, same cat smeared across time, same cat when the lights go out.
ideas.on_screen: Hologram opens on a glowing wireframe cat on a wireframe sofa ('here's your cat'). Every beat of the sim is the SAME cat, re-lit, multiplied or stretched, always unimpressed. The viewer's eye is never lost, so Maddie can talk at 200 wpm.
ideas.reference: Kurzgesagt, 'The Origin of Consciousness' and 'The Multiverse' style, one anchor visual per video: https://www.youtube.com/@kurzgesagt ; Vsauce 'How to Count Past Infinity' (one object, escalating): https://www.youtube.com/@Vsauce
ideas.risk: Do not let the cat become Schrodinger's cat; see the running-gag idea below.

ideas.title: Powers of Ten, then sideways (escalation of scale)
ideas.idea: Eames' Powers of Ten escalates by a fixed ratio so every jump feels earned and fast. Do it on the cat: zoom OUT x10 per half-second (room, street, Swindon, UK, Earth), then Maddie says 'and that's only ONE direction' and the camera goes SIDEWAYS through copies (multiverse), then along TIME as a new axis, then 'more dimensions of time than you knew'. The scale ladder is a grammar the audience already knows, so the left turn into time lands.
ideas.on_screen: Hard zoom-out ladder with a ticking scale label in Maddie's hologram font (1m, 10m, 100m...). At the top, a slam cut to a sideways dolly through a corridor of identical Swindons, each a different colour. Then the corridor becomes a ribbon (time), then the ribbon fans into several ribbons (extra time dimensions).
ideas.reference: Charles and Ray Eames, Powers of Ten (1977): https://www.eamesoffice.com/the-work/powers-of-ten/ ; Morrison's 'Cosmic Zoom' lineage
ideas.risk: Keep the multiverse as 'your physicists argue about this', not as settled.

ideas.title: One analogy per beat: the Flatland step and the brick wall of time
ideas.idea: Sagan used Flatland in Cosmos to make a fourth dimension graspable in about a minute; minutephysics and Hank Green use one hand-drawn analogy and then move on. Give Maddie exactly two analogies. (1) Flatland: a flat paper person cannot see 'up', 'you're the flat person, time's your up', cut to a flat paper Derek. (2) Growing block as brickwork: the past is laid bricks, the future isn't there yet, 'now' is the bricklayer's edge. Builder imagery suits the working-class reader and is literally the growing block.
ideas.on_screen: Paper-cut Flatland Derek in the hologram sees only a line of the cat; a hand-lift reveals the whole cat. Then a wall of glowing bricks being laid in real time by a tiny hologram bricklayer; behind the trowel is empty grid. Maddie: 'Back there's set. Out front's not built yet. Mind the gap.'
ideas.reference: Cosmos Ep.11 'The Persistence of Memory' Flatland sequence (Sagan, 1980) and Abbott's Flatland (gutenberg.org/ebooks/97); minutephysics one-analogy format: https://www.youtube.com/@minutephysics
ideas.risk: Brickwork must show past fixed and future absent only, not a block universe where the future already exists.

ideas.title: The 'but here's the weird bit' turn, with honest hedging
ideas.idea: Vsauce and Hank Green keep trust with a recurring pivot ('but here's the thing', 'and that's where it gets weird') and open hedges ('we think', 'people argue'). Use ONE hard pivot at the heart of the sim, and make the hedge a joke in Maddie's voice so it satisfies the 'never say the science is settled' rule without slowing down.
ideas.on_screen: Everything speeds up, then a record-scratch freeze on the hologram: 'But here's the weird bit.' The cat and every universe go grey and still except one glowing thread: 'whatever's doing the choosing... runs on you.' Hedge: 'Your best brains still argue about this. I'm a delivery robot. I just noticed it never worked without you.' Then it accelerates again.
ideas.serves: hologram scene / message (consciousness drives the universe, partnership)
ideas.reference: Vsauce 'But here's the thing' turn in e.g. 'Is Your Red The Same as My Red?': https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=evQsOFQju0s ; Hank Green SciShow/Crash Course hedging register: https://www.youtube.com/@scishow
ideas.risk: Must not slide into 'observer = mind' or collapse language. Say 'something was missing from every simulation' and 'it never ran without you', not that watching makes things real.

ideas.title: Running gag that defuses the forbidden science: 'Not THAT cat'
ideas.idea: Horrible Histories and Hitchhiker's Guide use one deadpan gag, repeated and escalated, to carry dense material. The audience will think of the box-cat; Maddie pre-empts it and the gag becomes the film's anti-superposition insurance. Each time a branch splits, the cat is in a different place doing something mundane, never in two states at once.
ideas.on_screen: Beat 1: a hologram cardboard box appears, Maddie swats it away: 'Nobody's boxing your cat, we're not animals.' Later in each universe the cat is simply elsewhere: on the roof, on the sofa, in a bin, always vexed. Callback in the ending: the cat sits in the clean room, alone, tail flick, nobody there. Hitchhiker-style one-line asides in a pop-up 'Guide' caption: 'Mostly harmless (the cat)'.
ideas.reference: Douglas Adams, The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy (deadpan footnote voice, 'Don't Panic'); Horrible Histories joke-per-fact density: https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b006mf4j
ideas.risk: Low. The gag only works if the cat never visibly occupies two places in one frame; keep branches as separate cuts.

ideas.title: One held breath inside the torrent (Sagan beat)
ideas.idea: The fastest communicators earn awe by contrast: Sagan's Pale Blue Dot works because it is slow. Hyper speech for 34 seconds, then ONE 1.5 second near-silence on the line that carries the film's emotion. It keeps hyperactive Maddie from reading as a gabble and makes the 'you lot aren't here any more' line land hard.
ideas.on_screen: Speech cuts; the hologram dims to a lone glowing Earth with all the human lights switched off, one slow push-in, ambient hum only. Maddie, quiet for the first time: 'And it needs you to drive it. And you lot aren't here any more.' Beat. Then instantly bright again: 'Anyway! Patrol's out, mind how you go.'
ideas.reference: Carl Sagan, 'Pale Blue Dot' (1994 reading, Planetary Society): https://www.planetary.org/worlds/pale-blue-dot ; Cosmos (1980)
ideas.risk: Do not let the beat grow past 2s or the 'sorry we killed you, moving on' tonal whiplash is lost.

ideas.title: Design the sim's last 6 seconds as a self-contained recap card (for the bunker TV)
ideas.idea: Bill Nye and Sagan end on a tell-them-what-you-told-them recap. Build the final seconds of the sim as a standalone 3-card recap that can be lifted whole and replayed on the bunker TV, so the ending needs no explaining and the vote is easy. Same words, same visuals, so the payoff is recognition.
ideas.on_screen: Three big hologram cards slam on, each with one icon and one line: 'ONE universe. It matters.' / 'It runs on you.' / 'The time machine needs you to drive.' with a cat-shaped cursor on the third. Later in the bunker, the old TV plays exactly these cards with a tracking glitch; Sandra reads the last line aloud.
ideas.serves: ending jeopardy / bunker vote / hologram scene
ideas.reference: Bill Nye the Science Guy segment close-out ('Consider the Following'): https://www.youtube.com/@BillNyeTheScienceGuy ; Kurzgesagt end-of-video summary cards
ideas.risk: Low. Ensure the card lines stay within 'something was missing' language, no settled-science claims.

ideas.title: 40-second running order for Maddie's simulation
ideas.idea: Applies all of the above to a timed beat sheet at roughly 3.5 words per second (about 130 words). Rule: one new idea per 5 seconds, one analogy each, one pivot, one held breath, one gag, one callback.
ideas.on_screen: 0:00-0:03 'I'll show you.' Whip-pan into hologram; wireframe Maddie, neon grid, a sofa. 'Here's your cat.' (anchor object). 0:03-0:08 Scale ladder: cat to room to Swindon to Earth, label ticking x10. 'Zoom out, nothing. Boring. So we went sideways.' 0:08-0:14 Multiverse corridor of near-identical Swindons. 'Maybe there's loads of you. Rick and Morty portal gun, Doctor Strange, lovely, very cinematic.' Cardboard box swatted: 'Not THAT cat.' 0:14-0:17 Record scratch: 'But here's the weird bit.' Grey freeze. 'Only the one universe, so it really matters. And so did you.' 0:17-0:25 Time: brick-wall growing block with bricklayer. 'Back there's set. Out front's not built yet. And your time? More dimensions than you were told. Flatland Derek only sees a line.' Ribbons fan out. 0:25-0:31 Everything lights up with a thread through it: 'Whatever keeps all of it going... never ran without you. Your best brains still argue, I'm a delivery robot.' 0:31-0:33 Held breath: Earth, lights off, hum. 0:33-0:38 'My boss built a time machine. He desperately wants to go back and fix this mess. But it needs consciousness to drive it. And you lot aren't here any more.' Recap cards slam. 0:38-0:40 Hard cut to street, bright, Maddie chipper: 'Patrol's out, mind how you go.'
ideas.serves: hologram scene / fast speech / message / ending payoff
ideas.reference: Synthesis of Kurzgesagt, Vsauce, Eames, Sagan, minutephysics, Horrible Histories, Hitchhiker's Guide as above.
ideas.risk: Dense: about 130 spoken words in 40s is hyperactive but intelligible only if each line sits on its own cut; consider trimming the Rick and Morty and Doctor Strange jokes to one line if timing fails. Keep every claim hedged and the growing-block picture one-directional.
